📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Grafana Begins Its Biggest UI Refresh Since Version 7.

Nov 27, 2026 3 min read.

Sources indicate that grafana Labs has introduced the first phase of its biggest visual refresh since Grafana 7, bringing updated themes, more consistent interface components, and improved visual hierarchy to its observability platform. Introduced as part of Grafana 13.3, the refresh is now available in public preview across Grafana Cloud and self-managed deployments.

Industry observers note that the changes address a growing problem as Grafana has expanded: years of rapid feature development have created design inconsistencies, competing visual elements, and different interaction patterns across the platform. Rather than introducing a complete redesign, Grafana is standardising its existing interface while retaining familiar navigation and plugin compatibility.

The longer-term objective is to make the platform easier to use as observability workflows increasingly incorporate AI assistants and agent-driven interactions.

Grafana's extensive growth has brought support for a broad range of observability use cases, but this has also introduced what the company describes as design debt. Different parts of the interface have evolved independently, resulting in inconsistent visual cues, component variations, and interaction patterns.

It has been revealed that the design refresh is intended to address these inconsistencies without slowing the platform's continued development. Grafana wants users to learn an interaction pattern once and apply that knowledge consistently across dashboards, panels, drawers, and other parts of the interface.

The work has also been influenced by the development of Grafana Assistant and Assistant Workspace, which introduced new interaction patterns for AI-powered workflows and prompted the design team to reconsider the platform's visual language.

Newly introduced default light and dark themes use redesigned colour palettes intended to improve accessibility. Grafana has also reduced the number of available component variations, helping standardise how common interface elements behave.

Typography, borders, shadows and visual layering have been updated to create a clearer information hierarchy. The intention is to reduce competing visual elements and make it easier for users to identify crucial information when investigating incidents or exploring data.

Sources indicate that these changes extend across fundamental interface components, including cards, panels, and drawers. Rather than simply applying a new visual style, Grafana is revisiting the underlying design primitives so that the interface remains consistent as the product evolves.

An interesting motivation behind the refresh is Grafana's view that traditional graphical interfaces will increasingly coexist with terminal-based and agentic chat interactions.

As more workflows become accessible through AI assistants, the remaining graphical interactions need to be particularly clear and predictable. People should be able to understand the information presented, recognise important changes and move between workflows without having to relearn different interface conventions.

According to recent reports, this makes visual consistency more than a cosmetic exercise. It becomes part of ensuring that engineers can work effectively across both traditional observability interfaces and newer AI-assisted experiences.

Grafana is deliberately introducing the refresh in phases, allowing users and contributors to adapt while providing feedback before further changes are made.

Importantly, the company describes this as a visual refresh rather than a complete redesign. Existing navigation remains unchanged, and the update introduces no breaking changes for plugins.

Self-managed users can enable the new styling through the grafana.visualDesignRefresh feature toggle and can switch back to the previous appearance if required. Grafana Cloud users can also access the public preview.

The manufacturer has encouraged feedback through its community Slack and an in-app survey, using early adoption and user responses to guide subsequent iterations.

Other observability platforms, including Datadog and Newly introduced Relic, have also invested in simplifying how engineers navigate increasingly complex monitoring environments. Grafana's challenge is particularly interesting given its open-source ecosystem, where plugins and contributions introduce additional interface requirements.

The refresh reflects a broader product engineering principle: as platforms grow, maintaining consistency becomes as key as introducing new functionality.

For observability tools, where engineers often work under pressure during production incidents, reducing cognitive overhead can directly improve how quickly they find and interpret relevant information.

Grafana's refresh is therefore less about changing how the platform works and more about making its growing capabilities easier to understand and use. As AI increasingly changes how engineers interact with observability systems, a clear and consistent graphical experience remains an important part of the overall design.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • SAP told CNBC that AI was rapidly changing its business environment, prompting continuous reviews of how its organization and workforce needed to evolve, and that roles and functions would change during its transformation.
  • Recent findings suggest that reuters independently reported on November 27, 2026, that two people familiar with the matter described preparations for a sizeable workforce reduction, with one saying the works council had not yet been informed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bloomberg reported on November 26, 2026, that SAP was preparing a strategy to eliminate at least 10,000 positions as it reshaped its software business for AI, citing people familiar with the matter, in a report carried by CNBC on November 27, 2026.

SAP told CNBC that AI was rapidly changing its business environment, prompting continuous reviews of how its organization and workforce needed to evolve, and that roles and functions would change during its transformation. Its statement added: “Beyond this, no decisions have been made regarding any further measures. We do not comment on speculation.”.

Recent findings suggest that reuters independently reported on November 27, 2026, that two people familiar with the matter described preparations for a sizeable workforce reduction, with one saying the works council had not yet been informed. SAP employs around 113,000 people worldwide. At the reported minimum, the reduction would be equivalent to roughly 9% of that workforce, calculated from the two figures.

Bloomberg’s account mentioned all departments had been asked to identify potential cuts, with product, engineering and sales receiving particular focus. The reported plan follows a 2024 reorganization that eliminated around 10,000 positions, primarily through voluntary exits and retraining. Hiring for new roles subsequently kept total headcount broadly flat.

In a recent development, CNBC placed the reported initiative against CEO Christian Klein’s push toward an AI-first strategy. SAP completed four acquisitions in 2026: Reltio, Dremio, Prior Labs and TechWolf. It also made strategic investments in AI-focused companies including Parloa, n8n and Conduct. Their stated purposes range from organizing corporate data and building models for business information to analyzing workforce skills.

Reuters also reported that Klein and Chief Financial Officer Dominik Asam had indicated at investor events that a workforce reduction was possible. SAP trimmed its outlook in July 2026 as AI-focused deals weighed on earnings, and an SAP executive remarked in October 2026 that the company was swapping some costly models used in its products for lower-cost alternatives. Those moves connect the workforce review to a broader effort to control the cost of SAP’s AI expansion.

According to recent reports, CNBC cited comparable moves with different rationales. WiseTech Global’s February 2026 plan covered about 2,000 cuts over two years as it integrated AI, while Atlassian’s March 2026 plan called for about 1,600 cuts partly to fund further AI investment. Cloudflare’s May 2026 plan involved more than 1,100 roles as it moved toward an AI-first operating model.

Challenger, Gray & Christmas’s October 2026 report shows that the broader U.S. trend is more mixed. Employers cited AI in 121,401 unveiled job cuts through October 2026, approximately 20% of the 617,189 total. AI was cited for 1,265 cuts in October, its lowest monthly total of 2026, while market and economic conditions overtook AI as the leading stated reason for the year.

Technology remained the largest industry category in Challenger’s U.S. tracking, with 171,501 announced cuts through October, up 21% from 141,159 in the same period of 2025 and accounting for 28% of the 2026 total. The contrast matters for SAP: its reported initiative is explicitly tied to AI, while the broader technology total includes reductions made for many other reasons.

For employees, the decisive questions are whether the reported review becomes a formal initiative, when the works council is informed, and whether SAP again combines voluntary exits and retraining with hiring for new roles. Those factors will shape whether the AI overhaul produces a net workforce reduction or another redistribution of roles while the organization absorbs the cost of its AI expansion.

Sources indicate that jade Orin is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI, covering artificial intelligence in human resources, workforce analytics, and organizational performance. Her work focuses on how AI is reshaping recruitment, talent management, employee engagement, and productivity across modern workplaces.

With an analytical and human-centered perspective, Jade examines how data-driven tools are applied to hiring processes, skills mapping, performance analytics, and workforce planning—while paying close attention to fairness, bias mitigation, and employee well-being. She is particularly interested in how organizations balance efficiency gains with ethical responsibility and trust when deploying AI in people-centric systems.

Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1280 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

In a recent development, the Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating Newly introduced Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

Sources indicate that the modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

In a recent development, neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

In a recent development, start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

Recent findings suggest that after profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

The table reveals which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

Industry observers note that in Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

In a recent development, the system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

It has been revealed that with @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

The table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

Sources indicate that key_averages() reveals which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

One of the most frustrating aspects of using the old autoencoder-based FaceSwap program (or the more popular DeepFaceLab, which had exactly the same concern), was trying to get a person to either look to camera, or not look to camera:.

According to recent reports, the IA Change Image tool is one of many, including functionality native to Photoshop in the neural filters section, that offers owners a chance to rethink eye direction. Source.

If the training data for the personality did not have enough ‘eye contact’, camera-facing examples, the model trained from it simply did not have the data to generate that eyeline, since it had discounted the few to-camera examples as outliers in the training data, during the training process.

Conversely, if one had used ‘influencer’-style videos as the primary data source, it would be practically impossible to get the AI persona to not look at the camera, since ‘eye contact’ was dominant in the data.

You would think the age of diffusion-based generative AI would have ushered all these issues away; yet recognizing, changing, and predicting eye direction remains a very dark art even now.

In 2023 NVIDIA’s Broadcast app offered eyeline-changing on demand, though it did not seem on launch to be a reliable or totally convincing solution:.

It has been revealed that A grab from the premium demo for NVIDIA Broadcast’s gaze-altering functionality. Even in this flagship example, the AI-altered version does not really look to camera properly. Source.

Industry observers note that photoshop included a Change Eye Direction facility in one of its Neural Filters even before the advent of Firefly GenAI in the program; but neither of these methods have ever worked very well. Likewise, asking even the best of the current frontier Vision Language Models (VLMs) to subtly change eye direction in a photo still obtains spotty results.

Recent findings suggest that photoshop’s gaze correction feature relied initially on cloud processing, since most owners lacked the GPU resources needed to perform the task locally. Even then, achieving a convincing change in gaze required considerable manual retouching. In both examples shown here, the original eye color has been poorly reproduced. In the Jennifer Lawrence example the iris is softly-rendered; in the Ryan Gosling example, the iris appears considerably smaller. Source  (The author’s own work at another domain).

According to recent reports, the problem is the very small amount of ‘action area’ involved in eye direction, both in the real world, and as a pixel-percentage of footage. Though I used to obtain some limited improvement in autoencoder-based genAI tools by specifically training eye-contact/averted paired datasets, that kind of approach is really pushing against the domain trends in the base model.

Diffusion-based models, unless diverted by ancillary mechanisms, tend to treat all sections of images and videos as equally notable; one can therefore imagine the sheer volume of variegated eye data necessary in a training set to draw the model’s attention to such a small section of the total available image space.

A number of research methods have tried to improve on the state of the art in this regard by leveraging secondary indicators such as audio cues:.

In the 2023 paper ‘Multi-Modal Gaze Following in Conversational Scenarios’ , audio is used as a clue to indicate eye gaze. Source.

Perhaps the most common and obvious proxy for gaze direction is head direction:.

According to recent reports, examples of head-based eye disposition guessing in a 2024 paper. Source.

But this presumption may be one of the main reasons for mis-prediction of gaze direction, since you never know when the owner of the eyes will be subverting it:.

A case – albeit a telescoped one – where head direction does not equate to eye direction. Here the lateral diversion is very expressive, and indicative of some kind of narrative event, and clearly should not be dismissed as an outlier. Source.

Recent findings suggest that another recently-adopted proxy for gaze-estimation is evaluating what events are taking place in a scene, and guessing from that context where the eyes of an individual are likely to be alighting. For instance, this summer saw the release of the paper TextGaze: Prompting Gaze Target Estimation with Textual Scene Cues, which uses a VLM to generate textual descriptions of a person’s appearance, actions and apparent gaze direction, to establish where the person is looking:.

Industry observers note that test results comparing TextGaze (right) with the earlier GazeLLE system (center). The addition of contextual information helps the newer system locate gaze targets even when facial details are difficult to discern or other elements in the scene are visually distracting. Source.

As one can see from the examples above, in some of the cases under test, guessing the eye direction would even be momentarily challenging for us, even though (for reasons of mating and avoiding or sharpening combat) this skill is life-critical for humans.

Following on from this research is a more recent outing, a collaboration between the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and Google, titled Gaze World Model, which attempts to predict where a person will look next in a scene:.

It has been revealed that from the new paper, test results using two clips from ‘It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia’. Yellow boxes identify the people whose gaze is being tracked, green circles indicate where they actually look, and red crosses indicate the model’s estimates. The second and third frames in each sequence show future moments that the system had to predict without seeing the footage. Source.

The system was trained on video sequences in which changes in people’s gaze could be associated with activity around them. The beginnings of a hand gesture, for instance, might be interpreted as an early indication of where another person’s attention will be directed.

‘Where a person looks indicates their focus of attention, and how their gaze shifts between targets reveals how that attention responds to a changing scene. Existing gaze target estimation methods largely operate frame by frame and do not model these shifts.

‘Gaze shifts are often driven by dynamic changes in the scene, which is the kind of information world models are designed to encode.’.

With only two seconds of footage, the upcoming model allows gaze locations to be be predicted throughout the following second, with greater accuracy than was achieved by competing methods, the authors contend. In tests against both specialist gaze estimation systems and general-purpose AI models, including Google’s Gemini, nearly nine out of ten upcoming changes in gaze were successfully anticipated by the new system, compared to fewer than eight out of ten by its closest rival.

GWM uses Meta’s V-JEPA 2.1 as a foundation. Unlike generative video models, V-JEPA was designed to learn how the physical world behaves from video footage, without having to reconstruct every pixel of a scene. Rather, its existing knowledge of movement and interaction was adapted to the specific task of gaze prediction.

Overview of the Gaze World Model. Current gaze is estimated from the available footage (blue), while future gaze is estimated from predicted changes in the scene (purple) from latent scene dynamics.

A shift in gaze was defined as a brief transition between two sustained periods of looking at different targets, as shown below:.

Sources indicate that illustration of a gaze shift from a person to an object. The subject (yellow dashed box) looks initially at the other person’s face before redirecting her attention to the sheet of paper. Minimum fixation periods and a maximum transition time are imposed to distinguish meaningful changes in attention from fleeting eye movements.

The three types of gaze shift studied were from one person to another; from a person to an object or other location; and from an object or other location to a person, based on the V-JEPA 2.1 methodology:.

Examples of V-JEPA 2.1 predicting upcoming human actions from first-person video footage. The colored boxes identify objects that the person may interact with next, with labels indicating the anticipated action and time until contact. Each set of predictions is shown alongside what actually occurred. Source.

Using the Scene-Head Interaction Module (SIM) from the earlier PaGE project, visual information about the person’s head was combined with information about the surrounding scene, and changes in both analyzed across successive frames.

Examples of zero-shot visual attention estimation from the PaGE study. Source.

During training, greater weight was given to parts of the scene undergoing the most visual change, since these could contain early indications of events likely to attract the subject’s attention. Both the future location of the gaze and the likelihood of a shift in attention were estimated – but not the exact moment at which the shift would occur.

For training and evaluation, the existing VideoAttentionTarget and ChildPlay datasets were supplemented with annotations identifying changes in gaze.

Examples from the ChildPlay dataset. Source.

Sources indicate that through a semi-automated annotation process, 6,204 gaze shifts were confirmed, with 15,086 video segments used for training. For this purpose, Meta’s SAM 3 semantic segmentation model was used to identify people and objects at the annotated gaze locations, with temporal rules applied to identify potential gaze shifts.

Subsequently, Google’s Gemini 3.5 Flash examined sequences of frames to establish whether the subject had actually changed their focus of attention, rather than merely blinking or following a moving target. Ambiguous cases were referred to human reviewers, and random audits of 15% of the annotations conducted, with a final sampled error rate of 0.5%.

It has been revealed that tests were designed to evaluate how accurately Gaze World Model (GWM) could establish where and when a person redirected their gaze in existing footage – and predict gaze locations and shifts beyond the observed footage. Comparisons were made with specialist image- and video-based gaze estimation systems, gaze forecasting methods, and general-purpose multimodal models.

According to recent reports, for gaze estimation in existing footage, GWM was tested against the image-based Gaze-LLE and PaGE systems, and MTGS, a video-based model designed to analyze social gaze. For the prediction of future gaze, the authors developed two implementations of the SAGE forecasting method (whose original code is unavailable) using the Sharingan Transformer architecture and PaGE to establish gaze locations.

Additionally, Qwen3.8 27B and Gemini 3.8 Flash were tested on both tasks, without additional training.

Training took place in two stages, initially using still images drawn primarily from the GazeFollow dataset, with additional material from VideoAttentionTarget, ChildPlay, and Multi-view Gaze Target Estimation (MVGT).

Industry observers note that the components trained to interpret individual images were then frozen, and the system trained on video sequences to anticipate changes in the scene and estimate gaze locations. Finally, these newly trained components were also frozen, and their outputs used to train the gaze-shift detection and forecasting modules.

Three sizes of the V-JEPA 2.1 visual encoder were used, frozen – ViT-B, ViT-L and ViT-g. Video clips comprised 16 frames sampled at 8fps, with gaze forecast for the subsequent eight frames. Training used four NVIDIA H100 GPUs, each with 80GB of VRAM.

Initial video training ran for 20 epochs with the AdamW optimizer, an effective batch size of 32, a peak learning rate of 0.0005, weight decay of 0.05, a linear warmup over 300 updates, and cosine decay to 0.0000001.

The gaze-shift modules were trained for 25 epochs using the same schedule, with a batch size of 64, a peak learning rate of 0.0003, and a warmup over 200 updates.

It has been revealed that test results for gaze estimation and gaze-shift detection in existing footage. The three variants of GWM (bottom) achieved the highest scores for detecting changes in gaze. Best results are in bold, and second-best results are underlined.

In the tests, all three versions of the latest model outperformed every rival at detecting changes in gaze within the observed footage, including the smallest version, with less than a tenth of the parameters of PaGE-H+. The largest version also matched or narrowly exceeded the best competing results in locating gaze targets.

About half of the improvement came from training the model to identify where a designated person in the scene was looking. The remaining gains came equally from tracking changes in gaze over time and predicting changes in the surrounding scene.

The two larger versions of GWM also tracked moving gaze targets more accurately than competing systems, with fewer fluctuations in estimated gaze locations, when the subject’s attention remained fixed.

Test results for predicting gaze locations and shifts up to one second ahead. The ‘Persistence’ baseline assumes that the last observed gaze location remains unchanged. Lower L2 scores indicate more accurate gaze predictions.

As shown above, the two larger versions of GWM outperformed all competing systems in predicting gaze locations, both half a second and a full second ahead, with gains of eight to ten percentage points in average precision for predicting gaze shifts. Compared to just extrapolating the last known gaze location, forecasting reduced average positional errors by 15.6% on VideoAttentionTarget and 11% on ChildPlay. Additional tests confirmed that accuracy deteriorated when the scene prediction component was removed*.

It has been revealed that it’s a testament to human acuity that a domain this small could be so dominant in survival, mating, and evaluation of all kinds in human life. Unfortunately, current trends in machine learning do not allow for an equivalent division and apportionment of attention when gathering and training a wider context of data, such as all-purpose image and video diffusion models.

Sources indicate that naturally, once you curate a face-only dataset, the eyes become a dominant feature and more can be achieved (though as I have noted, it remains an problem). However, it’s difficult to then apply lessons learned from that ‘close-up work’ to the wider context of integrated scenes, unless one intends to treat of the head separately – a clunky and Frankenstein-like proposition.

* We do not cover ablation studies, apart from exceptional cases, and therefore we refer the reader to the source paper for details of those.

Next Wave of Payer AI: Managing Regulations, Costs, and Fragmented Systems all at once

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1267 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Payer technology leaders are faced with AI sprawl – where system-embedded AI tools and third-party agentic AI platforms are promising faster audits, quicker decisions, and fewer manual interventions.
  • The NAIC put US health insurers’ aggregate profit margin at just 0.4% in 2025.
  • With these pressures mounting, Payer technology leaders must accelerate AI adoption and deliver measurable ROI within the next 6 to 8 months – without disrupting ongoing legacy modernization initiatives and ensuring regulatory compliance, including robust data security and governance across AI agents, knowledge, data, integration and platform layers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Payer technology leaders are faced with AI sprawl – where system-embedded AI tools and third-party agentic AI platforms are promising faster audits, quicker decisions, and fewer manual interventions. The demos look impressive, but due to workflow integration and user adoption challenges, we find that core operations staff are still manually gathering context, interpreting policies, coordinating work across multiple systems, and pushing cases through the same queues.

The NAIC put US health insurers’ aggregate profit margin at just 0.4% in 2025. Administrative expenses, meanwhile, went up by $5.8 billion. Blue Cross Blue Shield Association research estimates that more intensive hospital coding practices, potentially linked to AI, may be associated with about $2.3 billion in additional healthcare spending. Hence, rising administrative spend, investments in legacy modernization initiatives, provider and regulatory mandates such as price transparency and electronic prior authorizations are pushing Payers to move towards faster, more transparent audit decisions and optimized core operations.

With these pressures mounting, Payer technology leaders must accelerate AI adoption and deliver measurable ROI within the next 6 to 8 months – without disrupting ongoing legacy modernization initiatives and ensuring regulatory compliance, including robust data security and governance across AI agents, knowledge, data, integration and platform layers.

It has been revealed that today many Payer operations rely on siloed and disintegrated legacy core platforms and monolithic applications. Claims data, benefit documents, contract clauses, and medical records often sit in separate applications. Every process requires many manual touchpoints for information handoff and validation. An audit analyst or frontline operator may have to open several screens, reconcile conflicting information, and chase missing documents before a case can move forward. Adding AI to one step may save some time, but it does not optimize the overall cost or turnaround time if the rest of the process stays fragmented.

However, replacing legacy systems and workflows may not be a financially viable approach for achieving short-term ROI.

Industry observers note that an alternative approach is to enable AI-based coworkers that acts as virtual teammates to Payer operations staff and integrate with existing systems to gather relevant records, apply approved rules, identify missing information, and complete routine follow-ups. When an exception is found or there is a situation that needs human judgment, the AI coworkers can route the case to the right employee with the evidence and policy references attached. The key capabilities of an AI coworker are:.

Key Uses Cases: Audit Analyst (claims, prior authorization, FWA), Care Outreach Coworker, Member Services Coworker.

According to recent reports, auditors spend a fair amount of time just establishing whether a claim has been paid correctly. They need to check coding and benefits against provider contracts, while prior authorization reviews can get held up over missing documentation. Fraud, waste, and abuse (FWA) cases need detection of unusual billing patterns with perfectly legitimate explanation, but someone still has to examine the history behind it.

Recent findings suggest that an AI coworker can pull together the relevant records into the review and flag likely overpayments with supporting evidence. Auditors then decide whether to pursue recovery or raise a dispute, while qualified specialists retain responsibility for clinical and fraud judgments.

Industry observers note that A care manager calling a member may need to piece together information from several encounters to blueprint outreach or assign members to a CM/DM program. An AI coworker can take care of that preparation, leaving the manager with more time for the conversation itself.

Industry observers note that there are two potential financial benefits here. Care managers can reach more members without increasing staffing costs. Earlier engagement may also help lower medical spending, with care management programs showing fewer avoidable inpatient stays among members who engage early.

Member inquiries account for a regular part of a Payer’s operating costs. Even a seemingly simple question about whether a specialist visit is covered may require a representative to check network status in one system and benefits in another. If the information doesn’t match, the member may need to call again.

An AI coworker can pull the relevant policy and coverage details together while the representative is speaking to the member. More inquiries can then be resolved on the first call, reducing repeat contacts and the staff time spent handling them.

It has been revealed that the potential savings are clear in each of these examples. But there’s another cost to consider as Payers begin deploying AI coworkers across departments. A claims auditor and a member-services representative may both need access to the same benefit rules. If each team builds its own connections and maintains those rules independently, the Payer ends up duplicating the work and the expense.

Avoiding another layer of fragmented technology requires some decisions about how AI coworkers will be built, managed, and used across the organization.

Before committing to multiple deployments, Payer leaders need to work through six practical questions:.

Recent findings suggest that to realize early value from AI, Payer technology leaders should not wait for broader enterprise AI platform enablement or legacy modernization initiatives to go-live. The pragmatic next step is to choose one high-volume, high-impact workflow and get started with an AI coworker model. Once initial, measurable value is delivered and proven, then reuse the capabilities built during the first 100 days to expand AI adoption in adjacent areas.

This approach will help the organization gain a clearer view of what AI costs and what it saves, and they can start reconsidering how technology and services are contracted. While contracting with vendors, fees linked to agreed outcomes can become a more realistic proposition. And if the savings from one deployment can help finance the next, AI investment becomes easier to sustain. Payers could gradually build an operating model where each fresh coworker costs less to introduce, with more of the underlying capabilities already in place.

Industry observers note that shyam is an accomplished healthcare industry veteran with a robust 26-year career spanning Payers, Providers, Pharma, Life Sciences, and health IT segments. In his current role as Chief Business Officer at CitiusTech, he leads the Payer business and the organization's platform (IP) business. He is a member of CitiusTech's Executive Council, the senior leadership team responsible for company strategy and direction.

It has been revealed that shyam joined CitiusTech in its startup phase and has been part of the company's leadership for over 16 years – first helping scale the company across its early markets, then building the Payer business from the ground up into one of the company's largest verticals, serving some of the nation's leading health proposal organizations. He also heads the platform business, setting strategy and vision for PERFORM+, CitiusTech's proprietary AI-enabled clinical quality and value-based care platform and the company's flagship IP investment.

Sources indicate that shyam is a recognized voice in healthcare technology focused on Payer tech modernization, clinical quality, interoperability, and the intersection of AI and Payer technology. He regularly contributes to industry dialogue through conferences, webinars, and thought leadership.

Sources indicate that prior to CitiusTech, Shyam spent nearly a decade at Infosys. He holds a degree in biomedical engineering and lives in New Jersey with his wife and two rescue cats.

Tech Report: Hard Drive pricing has gotten bad

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ktz

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for years now, I’ve made it an annual tradition to replace one or two hard drives on Black Friday.
  • Industry observers note that but current hardware pricing is totally screwed.
  • Let’s take a look at disk prices over the past 8 years in today’s post.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for years now, I’ve made it an annual tradition to replace one or two hard drives on Black Friday. I typically run around ten physical disks, and swapping a couple out each year means I almost never have a drive older than five years in my systems. I’ve even previously made videos about shucking disks around this time of year.

Industry observers note that but current hardware pricing is totally screwed. So what is a lifelong self-hoster to do in times like these? With disk capacities increasing massively over the last 10 years I can now fit 20TB per slot. This means I could realistically go from ten spinners to five, and not really feel it too acutely. This will mean redoing my zpool layouts, which in turn means shuffling some data around as ZFS doesn’t like changes to the layout of existing pools. But, at these prices, I’m starting to think the hassle might be worth it.

Let’s take a look at disk prices over the past 8 years in today’s post.

The 20TB WD EasyStore I bought for $249.99 in November 2024 is, today, on sale, $549.99 this Black Friday. $300 more than 2 years ago for the same product, from the same store. It shows just how bad hard drive pricing has gotten (BestBuy 20TB listing).

Recent findings suggest that shucking is homelab speak for taking a perfectly good external drive out of its USB enclosure and sticking the SATA drive in your server. At $12.50/TB it was a fantastically affordable way to get massive amounts of storage. At $27.50/TB, absolutely not.

In November 2018 I bought five 10TB EasyStores for $179.99 each. At the time I wrote about doing the rounds of my local Best Buys to pickup more drives on Black Friday as quantities were limited at each location (My 2018 server build log).

Sources indicate that october 2023 was my best haul on a per-TB basis. Three 18TB drives put 54TB in my hands for $599.97. This year’s “deal” is fifty bucks shy of that entire order. Best Buy was still advertising those 18TB drives for $199.99 in November 2023. November 2023 deal archive.

In a recent development, buying refurbished or recertified enterprise drives used to be an easy way to bring the cost down. In August 2024 I bought four recertified 14TB Ultrastars from ServerPartDeals for $529.96 before tax. That was 56TB at $9.46/TB, even cheaper than the EasyStores and no shucking to do.

The sad truth is that across the board prices are up a minimum of 58%, and sometimes as much as 218% in just a year or two.

When the EasyStore is that bad, my first instinct is to shop around. Maybe I should try another retailer (to be clear I’m not blaming BestBuy for any of this), buy an enterprise drive, see what’s available recertified. But follow those listings back to the companies that actually make the drives and the choices narrow pretty swiftly. There are three major HDD makers left. How did we end up with so few?

Maxtor bought Quantum’s hard drive business in 2001, then Seagate bought Maxtor in 2006. Hitachi combined IBM’s disk business with its own to form HGST in 2003, and Toshiba bought Fujitsu’s HDD business in 2009. Seagate bought Samsung’s HDD business in December 2011, and Western Digital bought HGST in March 2012. The FTC required WD to sell desktop-drive manufacturing assets to Toshiba to keep a third supplier in that market. That left Seagate, Western Digital and Toshiba.

The 2011 Thailand floods hit while those last two deals were underway. WD halted production at all its Thai plants, and its average hard drive selling price went from $45 in fiscal 2011 to $62 in fiscal 2012. There was also a price-fixing case further up the supply chain. NHK Spring pleaded guilty in 2019 to fixing prices for the suspension assemblies that hold the read/write heads, and the court approved a $28.5 million fine. WD’s 2012 annual report · Ninth Circuit opinion.

Sources indicate that it’s hard to have anything positive to say in this post. The HDD manufacturing market is so consolidated nowadays - just like the memory market which is equally screwed - that it’s hard to see this as anything but mass market collusion by the HDD manufacturing cartel.

In a recent development, three companies is an awfully short list when you need to buy a hard drive. And with 89% of WD’s revenue coming from its cloud business in fiscal 2026, I don’t reckon those of us buying a couple of drives for a home server have much impact here. Just like with Nvidia and Micron, consumer markets just aren’t valuable enough so we have to make do with the crumbs instead.

As of November 26, 2026, the 20TB is 2.2× what I paid for the exact same SKU in 2024. It’s also $270 more than I paid for it in May 2025. And if you’re thinking you’ll just buy a smaller one, Best Buy’s 8TB Black Friday special is $299.99. That’s $37.50/TB and fifty bucks more than my 20TB cost two years ago. Best Buy’s EasyStore listings.

The jump gets sillier when you price a whole NAS. Four of those 20TB drives would have been $999.96 at my 2024 price. This week they’d be $2,199.96. That’s another $1,200 before you’ve bought a case, a board or a single stick of RAM. And the price per usable terabyte only gets worse once you set aside a drive for parity.

Industry observers note that if I can wish for one thing in 2027, it would be for hardware pricing to return to reasonable levels. I fear it may take a lot longer than that, though. So making do with less is going to be the upcoming normal for a while. And in that creative constraint, maybe we’ll have some fun along the way instead.

#161172. How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2230 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2230 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
  • Sources indicate that in an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
  • The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

Sources indicate that in an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

Industry observers note that the model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

Sources indicate that we rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

Recent findings suggest that the leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

In a recent development, the second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

Recent findings suggest that the natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

It has been revealed that to see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

In a recent development, this effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Recent findings suggest that think of a shipping manufacturer that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

In a recent development, and the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Sources indicate that adapting a model's vocabulary is not a newly introduced idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

According to recent reports, they choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

In a recent development, they work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

According to recent reports, first, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

In a recent development, to find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Industry observers note that third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents highlights up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

It has been revealed that A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

Industry observers note that to measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

According to recent reports, getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

Industry observers note that the lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

In a recent development, to find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Sources indicate that specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

Latest Update: AI Literacy Is the Missing Layer of Deepfake Defense

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (998 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, detection tools are getting smarter, but most deepfake scams still work because the person on the other end didn’t know what to check.
  • Sources indicate that in January 2024, a finance employee at Arup’s Hong Kong office received an email from the company’s UK-based chief financial officer asking for a confidential transaction.
  • It has been revealed that the incident is often quoted as proof of how convincing deepfakes have become.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, detection tools are getting smarter, but most deepfake scams still work because the person on the other end didn’t know what to check. That is a gap only awareness can close.

Sources indicate that in January 2024, a finance employee at Arup’s Hong Kong office received an email from the company’s UK-based chief financial officer asking for a confidential transaction. He was suspicious. Then he was invited to a video call with the CFO and several colleagues he recognized. The faces looked right and the voices sounded right, so he went ahead. He made 15 transfers worth about $25.6 million. Every other person on that call was a deepfake.

It has been revealed that the incident is often quoted as proof of how convincing deepfakes have become. That is true. But one detail deserves more attention. The employee doubted the request at first. His instinct was working. What he didn’t have was the knowledge that a live group video call could be faked, or a clear rule on what to do when a request from the top feels wrong.

This is where most deepfake defense plans fall short. Companies are investing in detection software and platforms are adding labels, but very little is being done to help everyday users understand what AI can do today. That understanding, or AI literacy, is the missing layer.

It has been revealed that for years, the standard advice has been to look for giveaways – odd blinking, lips that don’t match the words, blurry edges around the face. These tips made sense when deepfakes were crude. They make much less sense now.

According to recent reports, in 2025, identity verification organization iProov showed 2,000 people in the UK and US a mix of real and AI-generated images and videos. Only 0.1% of them got every answer right, even though they had been told in advance to look out for fakes. Yet around 60% of the participants felt confident about their ability to tell the difference.

Recent findings suggest that low accuracy combined with high confidence is the real risk here. Teaching people a checklist of visual flaws may simply make them feel safer than they actually are.

Recent findings suggest that detection tools are improving, and they have an key role to play. However, they learn from yesterday’s fakes while new generation tools keep arriving. Labels and watermarks help as well, but they can be removed. Moreover, many scams never pass through a platform that scans content. They arrive as a phone call, a voice note on a messaging app or a private video meeting.

Lawmakers are responding too. The TAKE IT DOWN Act, signed in May 2025, makes it a federal crime to publish non-consensual intimate images, including AI-generated ones, and gives platforms 48 hours to remove them once a victim reports them. Earlier, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) ruled that AI-generated voices in robocalls fall under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, opening the door to fines and lawsuits. These are meaningful steps. But laws act after the harm is done. They can’t stop a cloned voice that calls you at midnight pretending to be a family member, and they can’t help you decide in that moment whether to trust it.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, the financial stakes keep rising. Deloitte estimates that generative AI could push fraud losses in the US to $40 billion by 2027, up from $12.3 billion in 2023. McAfee’s 2026 State of the Scamiverse report adds that Americans see an average of three deepfakes a day, and one in three have lost money to a scam, with an average loss of $1,160.

Industry observers note that scammers are targeting people’s trust and everyday habits. That is why our defense needs to reach people as well.

AI literacy is often confused with knowing how to use chatbots or write prompts. When it comes to deepfakes, it means understanding three simple things:.

The last point is the most overlooked. The Arup employee had the doubt. What he lacked was the permission and a process to act on it.

Building this awareness doesn’t require a big budget. It requires consistency. Here’s where organizations can begin:.

Pro Tip: If a call or message asks you to act rapidly and keep it a secret, treat that as the warning sign, however real the face or voice may seem.

Firewalls protect networks and detection tools scan files. AI literacy, on the other hand, goes wherever people go, whether it is a late-night phone call, a family group chat or a video meeting on a personal laptop. It is also one of the most affordable defenses an organization can build.

We have spent years teaching people not to click on suspicious links. Deepfakes need the same steady effort, with a newly introduced message: what you see and hear online may not be real, and taking a minute to verify is simply good practice.

So, if someone on your team received a video call tomorrow from a senior leader asking for an urgent transfer, would they know it’s okay to hang up and call back?

A technology and transformation leader with 18 years in heavily regulated industries, she has built enterprise AI governance frameworks aligned with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, GDPR and the EU AI Act.

Netflix Builds Quasar to Measure the Blast Radius of Library API Changes

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (574 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Netflix Builds Quasar to Measure the Blast Radius of Library API Changes.
  • Nov 27, 2026 2 min read.
  • Netflix has developed Quasar, an internal tool that identifies which repositories use specific library API symbols, helping engineering teams assess the downstream impact of proposed changes before releasing them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Netflix Builds Quasar to Measure the Blast Radius of Library API Changes.

Nov 27, 2026 2 min read.

Netflix has developed Quasar, an internal tool that identifies which repositories use specific library API symbols, helping engineering teams assess the downstream impact of proposed changes before releasing them. The tool combines semantic code indexing with API comparisons to identify affected consumers, dependency versions, and relevant call sites across repositories.

Sources indicate that the challenge extends beyond identifying whether an API change is incompatible. Compatibility tools can flag a removed method or changed signature, but they do not necessarily identify which applications call it. Dependency graphs show declared relationships rather than actual usage, while text searches can miss references involving inheritance, overloads, and generated code. Building every downstream consumer to validate a change can also be expensive.

Quasar architecture diagram showing the indexing and query workflow (Source: Netflix Blog Post).

Recent findings suggest that quasar indexes symbol definitions and references using the SCIP Code Intelligence Protocol, an open format for representing code relationships. Language-specific indexers submit data during CI builds, which Quasar stores in Amazon S3 as Parquet files and queries through Amazon Athena.

Industry observers note that during pull request analysis, Quasar compares API definitions between commits and identifies added, removed, or modified symbols. It then queries indexed references to locate affected repositories, dependency versions, and source locations. A Netflix example indicates a deprecated method removal affecting 137 repositories across three library versions.

Example Quasar impact report showing affected repositories and dependency versions (Source: Netflix Blog Post).

However, an absence of indexed references does not prove that an API is unused. Reflection, dynamic loading, stale indexes, and incomplete coverage can prevent Quasar from observing every consumer.

Antonio J. del Águila, founder of Knaisoma, highlighted another limitation in a LinkedIn discussion about the approach:.

Observed usage has a blind spot for reflection and for code on rare paths, like a quarterly batch job, since those calls may never show up in the window that was sampled.

Roberto Pérez Alcolea, a member of Netflix's Java Platform Team and author of the original article, acknowledged the limitation and described ongoing work to complement static evidence:.

Industry observers note that reflection and incomplete indexing remain blind spots, and we’re also investing in runtime analysis to complement the static evidence. Together, those signals help inform removal decisions, without guaranteeing that an API is safe to delete.

According to recent reports, quasar complements Revapi for API compatibility analysis and Kythe for code navigation by connecting API changes with actual usage across repositories. SCIP supports usage queries across Java, Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust, while compatibility analysis covers JVM APIs and Protobuf changes traced through generated Java code. Netflix exposes findings through REST, GraphQL, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for developers and coding agents.

According to recent reports, netflix plans to move impact analysis earlier into coding workflows, allowing agents to identify public API changes and retrieve consumer information before pull requests are opened. The goal is to help prepare migration changes while keeping API and release decisions with library producers.
