Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3140 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done.
  • We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome.
  • ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Sources indicate that each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

It has been revealed that then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+.

In a recent development, so we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

According to recent reports, figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

According to recent reports, thinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

It has been revealed that if you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 indicates which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

Sources indicate that the executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

The headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

It has been revealed that average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

It has been revealed that the observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

It has been revealed that pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:.

Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

In a recent development, figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

It has been revealed that the move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

In a recent development, these results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

Sources indicate that figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

In a recent development, every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

According to recent reports, training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

It has been revealed that for the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each revision generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

Industry observers note that that explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:.

It has been revealed that no ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

It has been revealed that why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++.

Recent findings suggest that A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

Industry observers note that the question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

In a recent development, each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:.

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½).

Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

According to recent reports, we partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:.

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

Recent findings suggest that figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update.

In a recent development, figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

It has been revealed that when sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict.

Sources indicate that we release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training. The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are:.

Vikram Srivats, CCO & Head of Product Experience at WaveMaker – Interview Series

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2116 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vikram Srivats is Chief Commercial Officer and Head of Product Experience at WaveMaker.
  • Sources indicate that waveMaker provides an agentic application-generation platform for enterprise development teams.
  • Recent findings suggest that your career has taken you from handheld computing and wireless technology at Mindtree to IoT, enterprise software, and now AI-driven application development.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vikram Srivats is Chief Commercial Officer and Head of Product Experience at WaveMaker. His career spans handheld computing, wireless technology, IoT, and enterprise software. He focuses on the architectural and organizational requirements that turn emerging technologies into maintainable applications at enterprise scale, with an emphasis on code ownership, design consistency, and engineering discipline.

Sources indicate that waveMaker provides an agentic application-generation platform for enterprise development teams. Its two-pass approach separates AI-assisted interpretation of design intent from deterministic code generation, using a structured intermediate representation. The platform combines agent, visual, and code-editor workflows with reusable components and integrations designed to fit existing development practices.

Recent findings suggest that your career has taken you from handheld computing and wireless technology at Mindtree to IoT, enterprise software, and now AI-driven application development. How has that progression shaped your view of what it takes for an emerging technology to become genuinely useful at enterprise scale?

In a recent development, every wave I’ve watched from up close — handheld computing, wireless, IoT, cloud applications — seems to follow the same pattern. The technology does something impressive in a controlled setting. Then it hits enterprise scale, and the gap becomes visible: what it does in a pilot versus what it does reliably in production at a massive user scale, under stringent security audit, integrated with systems built a decade ago, and maintained by engineers who weren’t associated with the tech development itself.

According to recent reports, the companies who survive (and thrive) solve the hard architectural problems, not just the interesting, shiny ones. Enterprise scale punishes pure optimism and speed, and rewards discipline and rigor. A technology earns the right to be called enterprise-grade when it performs consistently, survives review, and can be changed by someone who didn’t build it.

Industry observers note that AI coding tools can generate functional applications remarkably rapidly. Where do you see the biggest gap today between code that works in a demo and software that is actually ready for production?

In a recent development, the gap is structural. Watching an AI tool generate a working UI in thirty seconds, you’re seeing the easy part: assembling recognizable patterns into something that renders. You’re not seeing consistent adherence to your design system, correct authentication and authorization flows, proper error handling across edge cases, clean integration with your existing APIs, code your security team can audit, or output another developer can modify six months from now without the original author present.

Industry observers note that the data backs this up. CodeRabbit’s analysis of production pull requests found AI-generated code introduces 1.7 times more issues than human-written code. Veracode’s testing found security vulnerabilities in roughly 45% of AI-generated output. Google’s DORA research demonstrated a 7.2% drop in delivery stability among teams using AI coding tools. The fix is the right architecture around AI that can actually guarantee quality and cost with speed.

It has been revealed that prompt-driven development has made software creation much faster and more accessible. What are the limitations of relying primarily on prompts once applications become larger, more complex, and business-critical?

Prompt-driven development is single-pass: describe intent, the model generates output, you hope it matches requirements. That works for self-contained tasks. It breaks down as complexity grows.

The core problem is that prompts carry no persistent context about your organization’s standards. An LLM has no memory of the architectural decision your team made many sprints ago — every prompt starts fresh. You get stylistic inconsistency across components, duplicated logic, security configurations that drift from established patterns, and a codebase that gets harder to reason about with each addition. Enterprise applications are living systems built on years of accumulated decisions. Prompts generate for the moment, not the long term, and that mismatch leads to architectural drift or worse, no architecture at all. If you were building a skyscraper, would you skip architecture and planning?

According to recent reports, generative AI is inherently non-deterministic, while enterprises generally want predictable and repeatable software. How significant is that tension, and what approaches can development teams use to control it?

Sources indicate that the tension is real. Non-determinism in a creative tool is a feature. In a compiler, it is almost a fatal flaw. Applying LLM-based generation directly to production code treats a creative tool as a compiler, and the results are predictably unpredictable.

Industry observers note that the architectural fixes: give the model a narrower, well-defined output space instead of letting it generate arbitrary code. Use an intermediate representation that validates intent before code gets emitted. Build guardrails that encode your organization’s standards so the model operates inside them. Non-determinism is valuable in the reasoning phase, figuring out what to build, and destructive in the generation phase, actually building it. Separating those two phases matters.

According to recent reports, waveMaker uses an intermediate representation and a two-pass approach rather than generating production code directly from prompts. Why do you believe separating AI reasoning from deterministic code generation can produce more reliable applications?

The two-pass compiler is one of the foundational breakthroughs in software engineering. Early compilers were single-pass: read source, emit machine code, hope for the best. They were fast but fragile. They couldn’t reason about the whole program before committing to output. The move to two-pass — separating analysis from synthesis — is what gave us the reliability and optimization that made modern software possible.

AI code generation repeated the single-pass mistake. WaveMaker applies the same historical fix. In the first pass, AI agents constrained by a Model Context Protocol (MCP, trained on a decade of production application patterns) convert design intent and natural language into WaveMaker Markup Language (WML): a compact, structured, language-agnostic intermediate representation that captures what the application should do without committing to how it gets implemented. In the second pass, a deterministic, template-based code generator converts WML into production-ready Angular, React or React Native code. Same WML in, same code out, every time. No hallucinations, no phantom dependencies.

The AI does what it does well: understand intent. The deterministic engine does what it does well: execute reliably. Neither phase carries the full burden of correctness alone. InfoWorld’s published analysis of this lays out the full technical case.

How should AI-generated applications incorporate an organization’s existing design systems, architectural standards, APIs, and reusable components rather than creating something upcoming with every prompt?

Every time a tool generates a slightly different button style, skips your established component library, or builds a fresh API integration pattern instead of reusing an existing one, it adds technical debt that takes engineers months to reconcile.

In a recent development, the fix is encoding organizational standards as hard constraints, not prompt suggestions. WaveMaker’s component library propagates design tokens from Figma directly, so your design system isn’t something you describe to the AI: it’s actually the space the AI operates in. API integrations via OpenAPI and Swagger get registered once and reused consistently. Security configurations — RBAC, SSO, OAuth, MFA — are set once and applied deterministically across every generated application. Your standards become the rails the system runs on.

Security, testing, version control, and CI/CD are already deeply embedded in enterprise development. How should AI application-generation tools fit into these workflows without creating an entirely separate development process?

Recent findings suggest that they shouldn’t create a parallel workflow. The moment an AI tool requires a separate repository, a separate deployment pipeline, or a separate security review process, it adds complexity instead of removing it. Enterprise teams have spent years building the practices around Git, CI/CD, and security scanning that make delivery reliable. Any AI layer that disrupts those workflows gets rejected, correctly.

Instead, AI generated code should live in your Git repository, run through your existing CI/CD pipelines, and get reviewed by your security teams using the tools they already use. There should be no proprietary runtime, no vendor-managed deployment, no lock-in that requires staying on the platform to keep applications running. The generated code should be yours: readable, auditable, maintainable by any engineer who knows the open standards framework.

Industry observers note that one concern with AI-generated software is the technical debt that may emerge months or years later. What needs to happen at the generation stage to ensure that developers can understand, modify, and maintain the resulting code over time?

According to recent reports, yes, technical debt from AI generation doesn’t surface immediately. This can be in the form of inconsistent patterns, undocumented assumptions, duplicated logic with subtle variations, and dependencies nobody can explain.

Recent findings suggest that what has to happen at generation time is disciplined structure. Generated code should follow consistent, recognizable patterns, because consistency is what lets someone who wasn’t there at creation understand it. It should use your established components. And if you have an intermediate representation, that itself is a readable artifact that an engineer who needs to understand why an application behaves a certain way can inspect and trace the reasoning back to the original design intent. That traceability is what separates maintainable generated code from a black box.

Most AI coding assistants have initially focused on making individual developers more productive. What changes when AI development systems are designed for entire engineering teams, including architects, designers, security teams, and developers?

It has been revealed that almost everything changes. Individual productivity tools optimize for one loop: one developer, one task, fast feedback. Team-scale systems solve a different problem. How do you maintain consistency across dozens of developers working in parallel? How do an architect’s decisions propagate to every component, not just the ones they personally touch? How do designers get a voice in the output without writing code? How do security teams set standards once and have them enforced automatically across everything generated?

That change from tools that assist to platforms that constrain productively, is the real design challenge. Architects, designers, developers, and security teams need different interfaces to the same underlying system. Architects define structural patterns. Designers watch their design tokens carry through every generated component. Security teams configure authentication once. Developers move between agent mode, visual mode, and code editor mode depending on the task. Everyone operates in the same system, on the same codebase, with the same standards enforced. Scale only happens because the platform was designed for teams, not individuals.

As agentic development matures, which parts of the software development lifecycle do you expect AI agents to take greater ownership of, and which decisions will continue to require human engineering judgment?

Industry observers note that agents will take increasing ownership of the translation layer: converting human intent into structured artifacts. Figma designs into component specifications. Business requirements into data models. API contracts into integration stubs. These are tasks where the input is well-defined, the output space is constrained, and correctness can be verified. Agents will also get better at producing a starting point that’s 80% correct and needs human refinement — faster and better than a blank page.

It has been revealed that what will remain with human engineers is anything involving competing values. Should this feature prioritize accessibility or performance when you can’t have both? Should this architecture optimize for extensibility or simplicity given where the product is likely to go? Should this security trade-off get made given the organization’s risk appetite? Agents can inform those decisions. They can’t make them. The most dangerous outcome of agentic AI is assuming that because an agent can make a decision, it should. The best engineering organizations will use AI to move faster on what can be specified, and preserve human judgment for what requires it.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to explore an AI-powered platform for building and modernizing enterprise applications should visit WaveMaker.

Breaking: Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package).
  • According to recent reports, the torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub.
  • In a recent development, the Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

According to recent reports, the torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

In a recent development, the Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We proposal to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Sources indicate that select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:.

No need for torchrun: the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:.

Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

According to recent reports, each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:.

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

#161155. Chris Radkowski, GRC Expert at Pathlock – Interview Series

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2842 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Unite ↗ Open Full Page

Chris Radkowski, GRC Expert at Pathlock – Interview Series

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2842 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chris Radkowski is a governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) expert at Pathlock.
  • Recent findings suggest that pathlock provides identity and access governance for ERP systems and other business-critical applications.
  • It has been revealed that you spent nearly 17 years at SAP leading governance, risk, compliance, and identity initiatives before joining Pathlock.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chris Radkowski is a governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) expert at Pathlock. He brings extensive experience in enterprise security, application access governance, and compliance, including nearly 17 years at SAP. His work focuses on how organizations manage access risk as business systems evolve and AI agents take on more operational responsibility.

Recent findings suggest that pathlock provides identity and access governance for ERP systems and other business-critical applications. Its platform combines access risk analysis, compliant provisioning, access certification, segregation-of-duties controls, and continuous monitoring to help organizations govern human and non-human identities and maintain audit readiness.

It has been revealed that you spent nearly 17 years at SAP leading governance, risk, compliance, and identity initiatives before joining Pathlock. How has your view of access governance evolved as enterprises move from managing human consumers to managing AI agents that can independently interact with critical business systems?

My time at SAP was about mastering a known problem of humans interacting with applications, requesting access, getting provisioned, and managers periodically reviewing whether that access still made sense. It was complex, but the actors were predictable.

Recent findings suggest that AI agents break that model and expose upcoming risks for organizations. They’re the fastest-growing class of non-human identities, and they don’t request access the way a person does. They’re granted broad, standing access and then act on it hundreds or thousands of times faster than any human could. That changes the core question of governance. For decades, we focused on controlling who could get into a system. With agents, the harder problem is understanding what happened after access was granted because an agent can execute an entire chain of transactions before anyone notices something’s off.

Industry observers note that pathlock research backs this up. More than half of organizations (52%) can’t fully verify what their AI agents are doing across business systems, and roughly half (48%) can’t trace agent activity end-to-end. That’s a governance gap is tolerable with machines because you had time to catch a bad decision. However, it’s not tolerable at machine speed.

Traditional identity governance was largely designed around employees, contractors, and administrators. What fundamentally changes when the “identity” requesting or exercising access is an autonomous AI agent?

In a recent development, everything about the trust model changes. Traditional identity governance assumed a person behind every request. Someone with a job function, a manager, a reason to need access, and a limited number of actions they could physically take in a day. You could build controls around that, such as role-based access, periodic reviews, segregation of duties, all calibrated to human speed and human judgment.

Sources indicate that an autonomous agent doesn’t fit that model. It’s not requesting access the way an employee does. It’s often granted broad, standing permissions up front so it can do its job across systems. And once it has that access, it can act far faster than any person could, executing chains of transactions, modifying records, approving workflows, all without a human in the loop at each step.

In a recent development, that breaks several assumptions governance was built on. First, who is requesting access stops being the interesting question. An agent’s identity doesn’t always map cleanly to a single person or role, and the same agent might act on behalf of different business processes at different times. Second, and more important, oversight shifts from access to action. It’s no longer enough to know an agent is authorized to touch the finance system. You need to know what it did there, whether that was appropriate, and whether you’d be able to reconstruct that trail after the fact. Furthermore, AI agents that act on behalf of the user are even harder to detect, since the activity appears as if the human user was behind the UI.

Pathlock research shows most organizations aren’t there yet. 79% have no dedicated AI governance team, and roughly half can’t fully verify or trace what their agents are doing across systems. That gap is really the core of the challenge. Governance built for human speed and human judgment simply hasn’t caught up to identities that act on their own, continuously.

It has been revealed that AI agents may need broad access across ERP, finance, HR, procurement, and other enterprise systems to complete complex workflows. How can organizations give agents enough authority to be useful without creating excessive privileges or latest security vulnerabilities?

This is really a least privilege problem at machine scale, and it’s the tension every organization deploying agents will run into. The instinct is to over-provision and give the agent broad access up front, so it never hits a wall mid-workflow. That’s exactly how you end up with an agent that can approve a vendor payment, alter that vendor’s banking details, and close out the transaction, when it only ever needed to do one of those things.

The fix is fundamentally similar to what we’ve always preached in access governance. Segregation of duties, least privilege, entitlements scoped to the task and the moment rather than standing indefinitely, but it must be automated and enforced continuously, because no human team can review permissions at the speed agents operate. An agent handling invoice matching doesn’t need open access to the general ledger, it needs exactly what that workflow requires, for exactly as long as it’s running. And the same SoD principles that apply to people apply here too. An agent that can both initiate and approve a transaction has recreated a classic violation, just faster.

None of that matters without traceability. Visibility into what an agent did has to be a first-class requirement, not something bolted on after an incident. Done well, tightly scoped, well-governed access makes an agent more useful, because its output can be trusted without someone double-checking everything behind it. The organizations getting this right are building governance into the deployment from day one.

Recent findings suggest that segregation of duties has traditionally prevented a single person from controlling conflicting parts of a business process. How should companies rethink segregation-of-duties policies when AI agents can execute multiple steps of a workflow autonomously?

According to recent reports, traditional SoD assumed one person, one role, and a workflow slow enough that a second person would naturally check the first person’s work at the next step. Agents dissolve that assumption. A single agent can be built to handle requisition, approval, and payment in one continuous run, which means the conflict controls we relied on for decades can simply be automated away, not by intent, but by convenience.

The rethink starts with applying the same logic to agents that we’ve always applied to people. No single identity, human or machine, should control both sides of a transaction that’s meant to have independent checks. In practice that means mapping SoD rules at the task level rather than the role level, so an agent that initiates a payment is structurally barred from also approving it, even if both actions technically fall under one automated workflow. It also means treating agent-to-agent handoffs as seriously as human handoffs. If one agent approves what another agent submitted, you need assurance that’s a genuine, independent check and not two instances of the same logic rubber-stamping each other.

The harder shift is monitoring. With people, SoD violations usually surface in periodic access reviews. With agents acting continuously, you need conflict detection running in real time, evaluating what an agent is doing across a workflow as it happens. Companies that only think about SoD at the point of granting access are already behind. The conflicts that matter now show up in execution.

Should enterprises treat AI agents, bots, and other non-human identities differently from human owners when it comes to provisioning, access certification, monitoring, and revoking privileges, or should essentially the same governance framework apply?

The underlying principles should be the same. Least privilege, segregation of duties, certification, and the ability to revoke access on demand. What must change is how those principles get implemented, because agents don’t behave like people.

Sources indicate that provisioning must be scoped to the task and granted in the moment. Certification can’t stay a quarterly checkbox either. A person’s role changes slowly; an agent’s effective access can shift with every task, so certification needs to be closer to continuous. Monitoring is the biggest gap today. We built audit trails around human behavior, and those baselines don’t hold for something executing thousands of actions an hour. Revocation must be instant and complete, since an agent with even a day of residual access at machine speed is a very different exposure than a slow offboarding for a person.

So, it’s less about a separate framework for agents and more about applying the same one with a much higher bar for speed and precision, since gaps close in on you far faster than they did with human identities.

Recent findings suggest that permissions tell security teams what an identity can do, but AI agents introduce a greater need to understand what they actually did. How important will continuous behavioral and transaction-level monitoring become as agentic AI adoption grows?

It’s going to become the center of gravity for governance. Permissions were always the easier half of the problem. They’re static, auditable, and change infrequently. What an identity does with those permissions was the harder half even with humans, and we mostly got away with lighter monitoring there because people move at human speed and leave a paper trail as they go.

Agents remove that cushion. An agent can be perfectly entitled and still cause damage, not by exceeding its permissions, but by using them in a way nobody anticipated, executing a sequence of legitimate actions that adds up to a bad outcome. That’s why the question must shift from “was this authorized” to “was this appropriate,” and you can only answer that by watching behavior and transactions as they happen.

Industry observers note that this is also where the traceability gap we’re already seeing becomes dangerous. Today, close to half of organizations can’t trace agent activity end-to-end, which means if something does go wrong, they’re reconstructing it after the fact rather than catching it in progress. As agentic adoption grows, that’s not a sustainable position. Continuous, transaction-level monitoring is what turns an agent from a black box you hope is behaving into a system you can stand behind, with a real record of what it did and why.

In a recent development, cloud migrations and moves to platforms such as SAP S/4HANA can significantly reshape roles, integrations, and permissions. Where do you see access risks most commonly emerging during these transformations, and how can organizations prevent legacy access problems from being carried into the latest environment?

The biggest risk is siloed governance during the migration itself. In a legacy environment like ECC, GRC often sits separately from the technical teams running the migration, and when that happens, organizations carry years of accumulated roles and risk straight into the fresh system rather than redesigning them. Our 2025 Digital Transformation & Access Risk Report found that 52% of organizations don’t proposal GRC controls early in the migration project. That’s the root cause of most of what goes wrong.

People tend to treat a move to S/4HANA as a technical upgrade, when it’s really a full business transformation. Roles get restructured, integrations multiply, and new transaction codes get introduced, so this is the moment to redesign access from scratch. Once bloated roles and stale SoD conflicts get carried into the new environment, they become far harder to unwind, because now they’re embedded in a system everyone assumes was built cleanly.

Sources indicate that preventing that means bringing GRC into the migration from day one. That includes running SoD analysis and access risk assessments in parallel with the technical build and giving teams real-time visibility into access risk throughout the transports moving from development through QA and into production. Organizations that treat governance as part of the transformation itself come out the other side with a system that’s easier to audit and maintain.

Industry observers note that many companies still rely on periodic and often manual user-access reviews. As the number of human and machine identities grows, do you expect access governance to shift toward continuous, automated controls rather than point-in-time certification exercises?

Sources indicate that yes, and I’d say it’s less a prediction than something already underway. Periodic, manual user access reviews were built for a world where the number of identities was manageable and roles changed slowly enough that a quarterly or annual checkpoint made sense. Neither of those conditions holds anymore. The sheer volume of human and machine identities has outgrown what any team can meaningfully review by hand, and a lot of organizations are still running that process through spreadsheets and email approvals, which was already a strain before agents entered the picture.

Recent findings suggest that point-in-time certification also tells you someone’s access was appropriate on the day it was reviewed but says nothing about the 90 days in between. With the pace at which access changes now, especially with machine identities that pick up new entitlements as workflows demand them, that gap is where real risk accumulates undetected.

Sources indicate that continuous, automated controls close that gap by evaluating access and usage as conditions change. That means the review becomes exception-based rather than exhaustive, with automation surfacing what’s changed or looks anomalous so people can focus their judgment where it’s needed instead of rubber-stamping thousands of unchanged entitlements. Organizations still doing this manually are working harder than they need to and are most likely to miss the access risk that matters.

Boards and senior executives increasingly have oversight responsibility for cybersecurity and compliance, but identity risk can be highly technical. What metrics should leadership teams track to understand whether access to critical enterprise systems is actually creating material business risk?

Boards don’t need technical details, just metrics translated into business risk. A few matter most. Open segregation-of-duties violations in finance, procurement, and payroll since those map directly to fraud risk. The percentage of identities, human and machine, covered by certification and monitoring, since ungoverned access is a blind spot regardless of how strong other controls are. And time-to-revoke, which reveals how long exposure windows stay open after someone leaves or a role changes.

I’d also add visibility into AI agent activity specifically, since roughly half of organizations still can’t fully verify or trace what their agents are doing. Together, these tell leadership whether access is genuinely governed or just assumed to be.

Looking ahead several years, as autonomous agents become capable of initiating transactions and making operational decisions across enterprise applications, what will a mature governance model for AI agents need to look like?

It has been revealed that A mature model must treat agents as full participants in governance. That means every agent has a clear identity, a defined purpose, and entitlements scoped to that purpose rather than broad standing access granted for convenience.

Sources indicate that access must be dynamic, expanding and contracting with the task rather than sitting as a permanent grant, and segregation of duties must be enforced structurally, so no single agent can both initiate and approve consequential actions. None of that works without continuous, transaction-level monitoring, since permissions only tell you what an agent can do, not what it did, and that distinction becomes the whole ballgame once agents are making operational decisions on their own.

Industry observers note that accountability also must be built in from the start. Every action needs to be traceable to the agent that took it, the data it acted on, and ideally the reasoning behind the decision, so organizations can explain outcomes after the fact rather than reconstruct them under pressure. And governance can’t sit solely with security teams anymore. It has to be a shared responsibility across business, risk, and compliance functions, with board-level visibility into how much operational authority agents hold.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to explore access governance, segregation of duties, and continuous monitoring for human and AI identities should visit Pathlock.

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1276 w)

Latest Update: Your AI Can Stay in the Country and Still Cross the Wrong Border

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1276 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Consider a US bank that has approved an AI agent to help staff review customer disputes.
  • Sources indicate that during one review, the agent needs to extract information from an attached document.
  • In a recent development, this is becoming a significant concern as enterprises give AI agents access to business systems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Consider a US bank that has approved an AI agent to help staff review customer disputes. The bank has chosen an AI model hosted in a US data center and checked that its deployment meets the processing-location commitments made to customers.

Sources indicate that during one review, the agent needs to extract information from an attached document. It calls a third-party tool that sends the document to an overseas service. The AI model stayed in the US, but the customer’s information crossed a border the bank never intended it to, and the agent may have done exactly what the employee asked. The problem lies in how the agent completed the task and whether anyone checked where the information would go.

In a recent development, this is becoming a significant concern as enterprises give AI agents access to business systems. An agent can retrieve records and call external services while completing a task, introducing processing locations that may not have been included in the original AI deployment assessment. NIST’s research on tool use in agent systems highlights how tool permissions and their ability to access external resources affect the risks of using them.

For CIOs, this means ensuring that every service an AI agent uses complies with the business’s data sovereignty requirements, even when an outage forces traffic to be rerouted.

It has been revealed that A bank may have agreed to keep some customers’ information in the US while allowing other records to be processed in approved overseas locations. Its own security policies may impose tighter restrictions. Those commitments must be reflected in the AI systems employees use, so engineers need to know which models and external tools can receive each customer’s information.

Industry observers note that AWS addresses this in its October 2026 Digital Sovereignty Lens announcement. Its guidance examines the infrastructure companies use, the third-party services they depend on, and where they store and process data.

According to recent reports, once the agent retrieves a customer’s records, it may pass a document to another service for processing. That creates a separate decision about who receives the information and where it goes. The employee’s permission to access the account does not necessarily extend to sharing its contents with an external provider.

It has been revealed that the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications identifies tool misuse and identity-related abuse among the risks that organizations need to address when agents take actions on their behalf. These risks require controls where the action occurs. Agents should have defined permissions for the tools they can use, and outgoing requests need appropriate checks before sensitive information is transmitted.

An AI gateway may govern requests sent to models, while an agent calls other services through separate connections. If those connections aren’t covered by the relevant controls, governing the model’s traffic will leave a gap.

You shouldn’t trust a service simply because it operates on an approved network. NIST’s zero-trust guidance for multi-cloud applications recommends checking the identity of the application or service requesting access and whether that access is permitted.

Sovereign AI adds another limitation to the supply-and-demand problem that AI infrastructure already manages. A firm might have several AI providers to choose from, but the best option for a request depends on what each provider can offer at the time. A cheaper model may be too slow, while another may already be struggling to handle demand.

For the bank, a fast, inexpensive model is no use if it processes customer information in a country the contract doesn’t allow. The bank also needs to know that whichever provider receives the request is authorized to handle those records.

Smarter routing applies those restrictions to each request. A destination that falls outside the customer’s approved options is excluded, leaving the system to weigh cost, performance, and available capacity among the eligible providers.

According to recent reports, the underlying policies still need to come from the business, and their enforcement must extend to the relevant model and tool traffic. Routing cannot protect a connection it never sees or compensate for permissions that were incorrectly granted.

I expect more enterprises and service providers to build these policy-aware routing capabilities into their AI control planes as AI traffic spreads across more applications and infrastructure.

The bank’s primary AI service goes down. Another provider in Canada could handle the requests, and under normal circumstances, switching over would make sense. But if the bank has promised that the affected customer information will be processed only in the US, that Canadian service is not an acceptable recovery destination.

AWS’s Digital Sovereignty Lens documentation recognizes this trade-off. Strict residency requirements can limit recovery options, creating a direct relationship between sovereignty and continuity planning.

The bank could prepare for this by arranging backup capacity with another approved provider or spreading its workloads across US locations. It could also have a different model ready to handle essential work if its usual service goes down, as long as the applications can use it.

When conditions change, the system can redirect requests to those approved alternatives without compromising the customer’s restrictions.

Sources indicate that there will still be situations where no compliant alternative is available. The business then needs an agreed response. Some requests may have to wait, while certain workflows could continue with reduced functionality or an approved manual process. For a critical service that cannot tolerate those interruptions, the business must invest in additional compliant capacity in advance.

It has been revealed that service providers will need to give customers reliable information about where workloads run and what happens when traffic moves between their facilities. Enterprises will need ways to express their own restrictions and apply them across the AI services they use.

Neither can assume that a model’s advertised hosting location tells the complete story. A request’s actual path may involve other services, and compliance records should reflect those interactions.

That requires the AI control plane to coordinate routing with access policies and information about available destinations. Teams should also record decisions so they can understand why a particular service was selected and whether applicable restrictions were met.

It has been revealed that I would encourage CIOs to test this using an actual agent workflow. Follow the request through the model and every tool the agent calls, checking which services receive customer information and where they process it. Then see what happens when the primary inference destination becomes unavailable.

Does the system use another approved service, or does it send the request somewhere the customer never authorized? If the team cannot answer that confidently, it needs to revisit the design before an outage puts everyone under pressure to get the service running again.

David Wang is VP of Product at Tetrate, which builds infrastructure for routing and governing AI traffic across enterprise and service-provider environments. Founded by creators of Istio and Envoy, Tetrate has deep roots in open-source application networking, service mesh and distributed systems. Its engineers contribute to Istio and Envoy, and the company co-created Envoy AI Gateway with Bloomberg, the project now known as Agent Router under the Agentic AI Foundation. David previously held vice president roles at MuleSoft and Databricks.

Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1282 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that LFM3 is our fresh generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence.
  • LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.
  • According to recent reports, LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that LFM3 is our fresh generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.

According to recent reports, LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:.

The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:.

Each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:.

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:.

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Sources indicate that reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a latest in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:.

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:.

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:.

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

In a recent development, reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:.

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:.

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

According to recent reports, reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:.

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:.

Recent findings suggest that for brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

Sources indicate that LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

Industry observers note that we adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

Meta Brings Code Review Auto-Approval More Mainstream with PyTorch GreenLight

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Meta Brings Code Review Auto-Approval More Mainstream with PyTorch GreenLight.
  • Nov 27, 2026 4 min read.
  • According to recent reports, greenLight has started letting a PyTorch AI reviewer approve pull requests from its own maintainers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Meta Brings Code Review Auto-Approval More Mainstream with PyTorch GreenLight.

Nov 27, 2026 4 min read.

According to recent reports, greenLight has started letting a PyTorch AI reviewer approve pull requests from its own maintainers. It is an open-source take on RADAR, the system Meta uses to land low-risk code changes without waiting on a human. The move comes as Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic and Sonar all describe ways to automate approval itself.

Sources indicate that RADAR stands for Risk Aware Diff Auto Review. Meta described it in a paper published in May. The paper starts from a capacity problem. Significant lines of code per human-landed diff rose 105.9% year over year, and diffs per developer per month rose 51%.

Meta attributes more than 80% of that increase to agentic AI assistance. Review has not kept pace, and the share of diffs reviewed within 24 hours is dropping. The authors describe their response in narrow terms.

Rather than attempting to replace code review broadly, RADAR targets automation to diffs that satisfy conservative safety criteria.

It has been revealed that RADAR sorts each diff by author and source before anything else. Deterministic codemods can be approved through a blanket policy and skip per-diff AI review. AI-generated codemods and automated runbooks go through a pipeline of safety checks, a Diff Risk Score and an LLM reviewer. Any failure sends the diff to a human.

According to recent reports, RADAR pipeline for AI and bot diffs. Source: Meta, "Automating Low-Risk Code Review at Meta" (arXiv 2605.30208).

The safety checks are hard limits. Open-source code, SOX-scoped code and code that needs extra review are never eligible. Runbooks must show a clean 60-day record, with zero production incidents and low revert and rejection rates. They are also capped at up to 2,000 diffs per day.

The Diff Risk Score works as a percentile gate. Allowlisted runbooks can land diffs up to the 50th percentile of risk. Other AI and bot sources stop at the 20th. Human-authored diffs default to the 5th, and each organization can tune its own thresholds.

The last gate is the RADAR Review Agent, which reads the actual change. It looks for safe patterns such as dead code removal, refactoring without behavior change, logging additions and new tests. The paper sets a strict bar for the agent.

For a diff to be auto-accepted, ACR requires a confidence score of at least 8 out of 10, with all changes classified into safe categories.

Recent findings suggest that approved bot diffs do not land at once. They wait in a landing queue for a configurable delay, shown as 24 hours in the paper's pipeline diagram. A human can still reject a diff during that window. Meta also monitors the funnel and tunes thresholds over time.

PyTorch noted in May that it would rebuild RADAR in the open. In a PyTorch devlog, Edward Yang wrote that "the RADAR approves are good" in Meta's internal use. He also set the rule that shapes GreenLight today.

RADAR is predicated on trust of the author, so RADAR approves will be limited to PyTorch maintainers who otherwise already have approval rights on the files being changed.

GreenLight follows that rule. Its cohort comes from the people listed in PyTorch's merge rules. A PR only gets a real verdict when a merge rule names its author. Everyone else is reviewed in shadow mode, and those reviews never become approvals.

Industry observers note that A scan runs every five minutes and sends eligible PRs to a reviewer workflow. A land verdict approves the PR and labels it. A no-land verdict withdraws any earlier GreenLight approval. The README adds that "a reverted PR is dropped from every path, permanently.".

Recent findings suggest that openAI described a similar policy at QCon San Francisco 2026. Brian Yang, member of technical staff at OpenAI, said a few engineers began building ChatGPT Ads with Codex in November 2025, and the codebase has zero human-written production code.

Yang matches approval to the change. Everyday changes are auto-approved once required checks pass. Critical changes must pass sandbox validation against a copy of production traffic, and then a human decides. His target is at least 90% auto-approval for routine PRs.

Industry observers note that the team tunes its automated reviewer every week. Engineers read past approvals, blocks and missed breakages, then test new thresholds against history. When too many bad PRs open, they fix the agent. When bad PRs keep merging, they fix the checker. Anthropic applies the same idea to the actions an agent takes while it works with its Antique code review system.

Sources indicate that sonar frames approval as part of what it calls the agentic software factory. Manish Kapur, VP of product marketing and developer relations at Sonar, wrote that in a well-run factory "the factory knows which changes can pass on automated evidence and which require a person to decide." Sonar's latest developer survey shows the pressure behind that. Of more than 1,000 respondents, 76% said they generate AI code faster than they can verify it, and only 39% always check it before committing.

It has been revealed that the common thread is scoped trust. Meta and PyTorch gate approval on author trust and a calibrated risk score. OpenAI gates it on the type of change, and Anthropic on what an action could break. In each case, reverts and misses feed back into the system.

Developers interested in learning more can read the RADAR paper here and find GreenLight's source here.
