📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Unite ↗ Open Full Page

Work, Workflows and Workforce: The Three-Part Approach to Evaluating AI ROI

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1297 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • CFOs need to explain what the business is getting from its AI spending.
  • In a recent development, I think about AI transformation in three categories: work, workflows and workforce.
  • Each category requires financial discipline, but the timing and measures of return will differ.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CFOs need to explain what the business is getting from its AI spending. That becomes difficult when the same conversation covers an employee using AI to prepare for a meeting and a multimillion-dollar effort to redesign customer support. Those investments have different purposes, and evaluating them against identical expectations can produce poor decisions.

In a recent development, I think about AI transformation in three categories: work, workflows and workforce. Work is how individuals do their jobs. Workflows are the broader business processes leadership must redesign. Workforce is how teams, roles and responsibilities must be structured to support those redesigned workflows.

Each category requires financial discipline, but the timing and measures of return will differ. CFOs should encourage learning where capabilities are still developing, demand measurable outcomes for major process investments and fund the workforce needed to deliver them.

According to recent reports, work starts with individuals figuring out how AI can improve their daily responsibilities. Someone in accounting might automate a recurring analysis. A marketer might use AI to prepare a campaign brief. These improvements develop from employees learning the tools and recognizing opportunities in their own jobs.

Spreadsheets are a useful comparison. Employees across departments learned to use them without relying on IT to build every calculation. AI requires a similar expansion of skills. Employees need enough knowledge to use models, build simple agents where appropriate and question manual tasks they have accepted for years.

Putting a precise ROI requirement on every interaction would make that learning harder. An employee may prepare for a meeting more effectively, but assigning a defensible financial return to that improvement is difficult. Early in adoption, finance should give employees room to learn and experiment.

It has been revealed that that still requires cost controls. CFOs can establish budgets, set individual usage caps and monitor consumption. Managers should track repeat usage, practical applications and whether employees are developing useful skills. User groups can help effective approaches spread across departments.

Industry observers note that as usage matures, finance can identify underused licenses and compare the cost of tools performing similar tasks. Trying to maximize adoption and minimize every dollar of spending simultaneously can stall progress before employees know what the tools can do.

The largest returns come from rethinking how an entire business process operates. Giving developers AI coding tools may help them complete individual tasks faster. Redesigning software delivery requires leadership to examine how code is written, reviewed, tested and deployed, including where work slows down between those steps.

That is an executive responsibility. The leader running the function must define how the process should change and partner with AI and IT teams on the technology required. Individual experiments alone are unlikely to produce that coordinated redesign.

For CFOs, these initiatives should carry the same expectations as other major software investments. Before committing capital, establish how the process performs today, the outcome management expects, the cost of achieving it and the period over which returns will be measured. The executive sponsoring the initiative should commit to those results upfront.

Customer support provides a practical example. Finance could measure cost per resolved case, resolution time and escalation rates, while checking that customer experience remains acceptable. In product development, relevant measures could include release velocity, defects and engineering capacity. The business case should connect those operational changes to the function’s existing priorities.

Industry observers note that that connection requires care. Hours saved create capacity, but the financial benefit depends on what happens next. Does the team handle more volume without additional hiring? Does it avoid outside spending? Can it deliver valuable products sooner? Faster output may create substantial value without reducing current payroll.

Industry observers note that finance and the sponsoring executive should agree on these assumptions before deployment and review them as the initiative scales. They also need conditions for modifying or stopping an investment that fails to deliver. Measuring ROI after a major rollout leaves too much room for shifting expectations.

As AI changes how work gets done, leaders need to reconsider how teams are organized. Responsibilities, reporting relationships and handoffs designed around manual processes may no longer fit. Workforce transformation means adjusting those structures so teams can deliver the outcomes promised by redesigned workflows.

Consider customer support. As AI handles more routine requests, leaders may need to shift people toward complex cases, oversight of automated responses and improvements to the support process. In engineering, faster code generation may require a different balance between writing code and reviewing, testing and deploying it.

According to recent reports, these changes should be planned alongside the workflow redesign. Leaders need to decide who owns the process, where human judgment is required and how teams will coordinate as responsibilities shift. Automating tasks while retaining every existing handoff can leave the broader process slow and expensive.

CFOs should test whether the proposed team structure supports the investment case. If AI creates capacity in one part of a process, can another team absorb the additional volume? Will employees move into higher-value work, or will capacity sit unused? The financial return depends on how effectively leaders reorganize work around that capacity.

Hiring and upskilling should support the roles those workflows require. Finance should include training and transition costs in the investment blueprint, then assess whether the upcoming structure improves throughput, service quality or cost per outcome. That connects workforce decisions directly to the returns expected from AI.

Industry observers note that the framework also helps CFOs evaluate where AI capabilities should come from. Start with functionality already available in existing software. If that cannot meet the need, assess other products built for the task. Custom development should follow a clear assessment of whether available solutions can deliver the required outcome.

It has been revealed that building a replacement for an established system can introduce maintenance obligations and technical debt alongside the initial development expense. Finance should compare total ownership costs, including integration, model consumption, security, human oversight and ongoing support. The objective is to improve the process at a sustainable cost.

AI belongs within the overall software investment discussion. Finance has long weighed the cost of technology against the people and resources required to perform the work. Variable charges tied to model usage or agent activity make it especially important to understand how costs change as adoption and transaction volumes grow.

Boards should see that distinction in reporting. Everyday tools warrant a view of adoption, learning and spending controls. Major workflow investments need a view of operational outcomes and financial returns against commitments. Workforce investments need evidence that the skills and organizational changes required for those returns are taking hold.

CFOs can use work, workflows and workforce to make better funding decisions across the AI portfolio. Give employees a controlled opportunity to learn, hold executives accountable for process improvements and invest in the people required to sustain them. That gives finance a clearer basis for deciding where AI spending should grow and where it should be reconsidered.

Michael Agresta is the chief financial officer of Coupa, a software firm that helps businesses manage their spending. Before joining Coupa in 2024, he served as CFO of Pluralsight, where he led finance, accounting, procurement, and tax. Earlier in his career, Agresta led finance at retail analytics company Skupos and worked on mergers and acquisitions at Deloitte.

Breaking: Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • They write, summarize, translate, and call tools.
  • In a recent development, say a customer calls your support line.
  • In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

In a recent development, say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they mentioned (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Today we're announcing two packages:.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's newly introduced speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

In a recent development, it's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:.

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:.

Industry observers note that the steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:.

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

In a recent development, to add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:.

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Industry observers note that downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

Industry observers note that when you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who remarked what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:.

Recent findings suggest that the diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:.

Recent findings suggest that parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

Recent findings suggest that these numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

Industry observers note that anyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't latest, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

Sources indicate that what's newly introduced is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

In a recent development, apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:.

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

According to recent reports, if you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Sources indicate that emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:.

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:.

According to recent reports, you use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Industry observers note that raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

In a recent development, language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

AnyDecisionModel has six backends:.

Recent findings suggest that the next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Sources indicate that like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

In a recent development, both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

Add the packages to your Package.swift:.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Recent findings suggest that each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Complications and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

#161135. Your VBC Strategy Is Your AI Strategy: Why Readiness for Both Is Aligning

Your VBC Strategy Is Your AI Strategy: Why Readiness for Both Is Aligning

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1541 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, healthcare has been treating AI readiness and value-based care (VBC) readiness as separate journeys, but they are the same one.
  • In a recent development, many healthcare organizations have been on a multi-year shift away from a system where profits are tied to care volume to one where incentives align with outcomes.
  • AI promises better care, lower costs, and improved outcomes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, healthcare has been treating AI readiness and value-based care (VBC) readiness as separate journeys, but they are the same one. The data foundation, governance, and cross-organization collaboration necessary to succeed in VBC are exactly what AI needs to deliver results, and the organizations that recognize this will move faster than those that do not.

In a recent development, many healthcare organizations have been on a multi-year shift away from a system where profits are tied to care volume to one where incentives align with outcomes. In 2024, 45% of all U.S. healthcare payments flowed through an alternative payment model (APM) contract, and nearly 30% were part of a downside risk contract. This shift will continue to accelerate as cost pressures mount and technology offers more opportunities to provide higher-quality care at a lower cost.

AI promises better care, lower costs, and improved outcomes. The global AI in healthcare market is valued at $36.7 billion in 2025 and projected to grow to $505.6 billion in 2033, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of nearly 40%. Yet most organizations are struggling to scale it. They are running into obstacles that make broad adoption difficult, and the same challenges showing up in their AI strategy have complicated the industry’s transition to VBC, namely:.

But there is also good news, because organizations that have already built capabilities to support VBC are uniquely positioned to realize meaningful results and ROI on their AI initiatives.

According to recent reports, AI holds promise to improve U.S. healthcare in multiple ways, from streamlining manual workflows and repeatable tasks to recommending appropriate treatment pathways based on unique patient needs. But not all the things these upcoming technologies can provide will require the same capabilities. Administrative AI tools can dramatically improve efficiency and produce measurable benefits within an organization, with capabilities like summarizing and managing data, automating processes like prior authorizations, and assisting in simple or repeatable tasks (for example, IT support or notetaking during patient encounters).

Outcome-focused tools—the ones essential for VBC success—need more advanced capabilities to predict outcomes, intervene earlier to reduce preventable clinical encounters or expenses, anticipate and stratify risk in patient populations, and improve both clinical and financial results. This type of AI requires an ecosystem built to support data sharing, interoperability, and collaboration. While many healthcare organizations have made significant progress in areas of interoperability and collaboration, 2023 data from the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC) shows that less than half (42%) of hospitals report clinicians routinely using clinical information from outside providers when treating patients, despite more than 70% having access to that information. Progress toward full interoperability remains disjointed and slow.

While many payers and providers have launched AI pilot programs, evaluated vendors, and explored point solutions and large language models, there is still only limited enterprise-scale deployment among organizations.

At the IndustryDive AI in Healthcare virtual event, Mutaz Shegwei, Senior Research Director, shared findings from IDC’s Worldwide Healthcare Provider AI and IT Investment Survey (September 2026) showing that only 12.6% of healthcare organizations describe their AI strategy as fully scaled. Nearly half remain in ad-hoc or emerging stages of adoption, particularly when it comes to measuring success. Three capabilities consistently emerged as important to the ability to scale AI in the future: a comprehensive data platform, enterprise-wide governance, and formal measurement of outcomes.

The IDC research found that 43.4% of providers either have or are planning comprehensive data platforms that integrate internal and external information, while a similar percentage have established or intend to establish AI governance councils. Fewer than one in four organizations (22.7%) measure AI’s impact through a formal enterprise-wide program, and without measurement there is no “proof of value” for these initiatives. The gap isn’t in ambition or technology—it’s in the foundation.

Historically, healthcare organizations have treated AI transformation and value-based care initiatives as separate and parallel efforts, with different budgets, leadership structures, and objectives. That approach is now holding both efforts back. By aligning AI and VBC data readiness efforts, payers and providers will have the foundation necessary to optimize organizational efficiency, clinical care delivery, and patient outcomes.

A recent survey of payer executives found that 66% do not have the data infrastructure and technology in place to support AI-driven decision making. Additionally, 92% mentioned that not having a single, connected data source is a major barrier to scaling AI in VBC initiatives.

Healthcare organizations often possess vast amounts of information, including claims, pharmacy, laboratory, eligibility, financial, and provider data. The challenge is not data availability but transforming that information into a trusted, usable asset. Rather than fixing these problems, AI systems amplify underlying data strengths and weaknesses. If datasets are incomplete, inconsistent, delayed, or fragmented, AI models bring out those shortcomings rather than resolve them.

This dynamic closely mirrors the requirements of value-based care, where success depends on the ability to track quality, cost, utilization, and risk through data. Organizations that have already invested in population health analytics, provider performance measurement, longitudinal patient records, and care management already have much of the foundation to support advanced AI applications.

An intertwined strategic approach to AI and VBC also improves specific operational workflows. Care coordination, risk stratification, and prior authorization are all areas where both providers and payers are actively deploying AI capabilities. Outcomes in these domains depend heavily on shared information and aligned incentives between organizations—the ability to collaborate and share clean, enriched data from a single source of truth.

Stop funding AI and VBC as separate programs. Align planning, governance, and budget under one strategy.

If the goal of deploying AI is simply to comb through volumes of data and interpret it in a report, healthcare organizations may have dozens of options from which to choose. Many AI tools can successfully identify patterns in a dataset. But for organizations that want their AI to take the next step toward identifying risks and opportunities, and suggesting options for intervention, the AI must have appropriate context.

In a recent development, A broad understanding of organizational goals, program incentives, population health and risks, and operational realities will ensure that an organization gets appropriate outputs from its AI. For example, if two separate employers are examining their diabetes-related risk and looking at interventions for their employees that will help meet VBC goals, it’s critical that the AI they use understands factors unique to their organization.

In a recent development, an employer with a highly transient workforce would be more interested in diabetes interventions that produce measurable short-term results, while a second employer with a long-tenured workforce may benefit from diabetes programs that take longer but produce better long-term health results. Organizations that are already optimizing for VBC—accounting for variables like patient populations, provider relationships, and incentive structures—would understand these contextual nuances and could apply a similar structure to their AI. The same model, deployed without context, gives both employers the wrong answer.

Administrative efficiency is a critical part of improving U.S. healthcare, but the true promise for AI in the industry lies in its ability to anticipate disease, mitigate preventable utilization, predict risk, and provide a path forward to improve patient health while reducing costs. That’s also the central premise for pursuing VBC programs and contracts. AI and VBC programs both require a strategic approach to ensure appropriate human oversight that can optimize outcomes, monitor results, and improve performance. Rather than choosing between an AI or a VBC roadmap, or pursuing them as separate strategic priorities, leaders can start by:.

The healthcare organizations that can succeed in their AI efforts won’t necessarily be the ones with the most AI pilot programs or the most advanced models and technology. It will be the organizations that align their AI and VBC efforts to ensure both are built around strong governance, interconnected systems, and a trusted data foundation.

David Morris has over 30 years of operational and executive leadership experience at blue chip companies throughout the healthcare ecosystem.

David drives client success across the value-based healthcare landscape by addressing the technology and service needs of the Payer, Provider, Employer, Pharma and Retail markets. He serves as EVP and Chief Commercial Officer with oversight of all commercial efforts, including Market Strategy, Sales and Client Success Management.

Prior to joining Cedar Gate Technologies, David held key leadership roles as EVP and Chief Commercial Officer with Citra Health Solutions, Chief Revenue Officer with Eliza Corporation (acquired by HMS Holdings), Senior Vice President of Global Sales and Services with Bupa Health Dialog (acquired by Rite Aid), National Vice President of Healthcare for SAP America, IMS Health (acquired by IQVIA), Baxter and George Washington University (GWU) Medical Center.

David received his undergraduate degree from George Washington University’s School of Government and Business Administration and now resides in Florida.

OpenAI Countersues Apple Over Alleged Hardware Trade-Secret Theft

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (974 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • OpenAI Group PBC, io Products, Chang Liu and Tang Yew Tan filed counterclaims against Apple on November 27, 2026, in California federal court, alleging that Apple misappropriated confidential hardware designs and manufacturing records.
  • Apple began the underlying case in the U.S.
  • According to recent reports, the central fresh allegation concerns an operations employee identified only as Employee X, who OpenAI says joined from Apple on December 2, 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI Group PBC, io Products, Chang Liu and Tang Yew Tan filed counterclaims against Apple on November 27, 2026, in California federal court, alleging that Apple misappropriated confidential hardware designs and manufacturing records. The accompanying answer denies Apple’s trade-secret and contract claims, while the counterclaims contain 12 causes of action.

Apple began the underlying case in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California on July 10, 2026, alleging trade-secret misappropriation and breaches of Intellectual Property Agreements. The defendants admit Liu’s and Tan’s employment histories and current OpenAI roles but deny stealing Apple’s trade secrets.

According to recent reports, the central fresh allegation concerns an operations employee identified only as Employee X, who OpenAI says joined from Apple on December 2, 2025. He initially handled camera and optics quality before his responsibilities expanded to enclosures, finishing, inspection and manufacturing quality; his last day at OpenAI was June 2, 2026.

The counterclaims describe transfers to personal email accounts and phone numbers, including a 76-page supplier measurement and inspection procedure sent on February 5, 2026. The materials allegedly included design geometry, manufacturing measurements, finishing criteria, supplier-performance results and inspection software. On June 1, 2026, Employee X sent six archives to a personal Singapore number, including structure.zip and CPK_GRR.zip, containing unreleased-device geometry, enclosure measurements, process-capability records and gauge analyses.

OpenAI alleges that Employee X rejoined Apple and, on information and belief, briefed senior Apple Asia-Pacific Operations personnel in July 2026 on its confidential hardware work and unreleased-product roadmap at Apple’s request. OpenAI sent Apple a cease-and-desist letter on October 9, 2026, requesting an investigation, preservation, containment and an accounting.

OpenAI notes the records’ value comes from specific engineering and production work rather than ordinary supplier identities: access to designs, test results and failure analyses could let a competitor avoid unsuccessful trials, qualify manufacturing methods sooner and anticipate production problems. The federal claim targets Apple’s alleged knowing acquisition, use or disclosure of that information through Employee X.

The filing separately alleges that Apple’s supply-management personnel pressured shared vendors to identify OpenAI projects and the names, locations and assignments of workers with Apple experience. Suppliers feared losing Apple allocations if they supported OpenAI. For many specialized functions, OpenAI has only one or two qualified suppliers, making interrupted capacity difficult to replace promptly.

Sources indicate that one finishing supplier allegedly moved OpenAI’s work on a general-purpose anodizing line, a shared metal-finishing process, to a separate overnight shift after Apple objected to OpenAI devices being processed in the same area or at the same time as Apple work. The change increased costs for the supplier and OpenAI. A second manufacturer allegedly withdrew from planned work because of threats from Apple, forcing OpenAI to revamp operations, staffing and contracting. The interference claim concerns actual disruption of existing purchasing and manufacturing commitments, rather than merely lost future orders.

The counterclaims also challenge Apple’s broad contractual definition of proprietary information and a one-year restriction on soliciting Apple employees or contractors after departure. Liu and Tan argue that California’s protection against contracts restraining lawful work prevents those terms from reaching general skills, public information or lawful recruiting.

OpenAI says 400 Apple employees have left for OpenAI and that Apple’s account and enforcement practices deter further hiring. Tan, who worked at Apple for approximately 24 years and is now OpenAI’s Chief Hardware Officer for Consumer Products, seeks declarations that his agreement cannot bar use of public information, general skills or lawful recruiting.

According to recent reports, liu alleges that Apple encouraged employees to mix work files and communications with personal iCloud and iMessage accounts, then used the resulting access after departures. After leaving Apple on January 22, 2026, he allowed his personal iCloud account to remain signed in on a returned Apple device solely so his former manager could retrieve Apple work files. His permission did not extend to review of his personal data.

They also underpin OpenAI’s unfair-competition claim that the prospect of post-departure monitoring deters engineers from moving to a competitor.

Sources indicate that the counterclaim plaintiffs request compensatory damages where permitted, reasonable royalties or statutory relief for trade-secret misappropriation, restitution, attorneys’ fees and narrowly tailored injunctions against established ongoing or threatened unlawful conduct. They also demand a jury trial.

The counterclaims broaden the case beyond files retained during employee departures. They put the infrastructure behind OpenAI’s unreleased hardware effort—supplier capacity, recruiting and the boundary between work and personal accounts—into the same judicial examination of whether either organization unlawfully obtained the other’s information.

Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • It has been revealed that there are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

It has been revealed that there are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

According to recent reports, mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super vital for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Sources indicate that mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That stated, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

Industry observers note that for each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Industry observers note that mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Sources indicate that cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

According to recent reports, the Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

The $30,000 average wedding figure you see everywhere is misleading. That number is skewed upward by luxury weddings in expensive metros like New York, San Francisco, and Los Angeles. The national median — the number where half of weddings cost more and half cost less — sits closer to $10,000 to $15,000. That distinction matters because it means a beautiful, memorable wedding is absolutely possible without spending five figures you do not have.

The FI perspective adds another layer: every dollar spent on a wedding is a dollar that cannot compound for decades. A $30,000 wedding invested for 30 years at a 7% average annual return grows to roughly $228,000. That does not mean you should elope in a courthouse (unless you want to), but it does mean you should spend intentionally on the categories that matter most to you and cut ruthlessly everywhere else.

Here is where the typical wedding dollar goes:.

The biggest takeaway from this table: venue and catering are 60-70% of the total. If you can reduce those two categories, you change the entire math.

Not all wedding spending creates equal memories. Research consistently shows that couples remember three things most vividly years later: the ceremony itself, the food and drinks, and the photographs. Almost nobody remembers the chair covers, the napkin folds, or the custom monogram on the cocktail napkins.

That insight creates a clear FI-aligned strategy: splurge on what creates lasting memories (photographer, food, music) and minimize everything else.

In a recent development, the golden rule of wedding budgeting: if you cannot remember whether a detail was present at the last three weddings you attended, your guests will not notice either. Cut it without guilt.

In a recent development, the biggest financial mistake couples make is not setting a firm budget before visiting any vendors. Venues and vendors are skilled at upselling, and without a hard number in mind, costs spiral rapidly. Start with a number you can pay in cash — wedding debt is one of the worst ways to begin a marriage and a direct threat to your FI timeline.

Follow this payment timeline to manage cash flow without credit card debt:.

Industry observers note that A practical savings strategy: divide your total budget by the number of months until the wedding and automate that transfer to a dedicated savings account. If your budget is $15,000 and your wedding is 15 months away, that is $1,000 per month. Treat it like any other savings goal on your FI path — automate, do not touch, and watch it grow.

Industry observers note that for couples on the FI path, consider this reframe: every dollar you shave from the wedding budget is a dollar that starts compounding immediately. Cutting $5,000 from a $20,000 wedding and investing that savings at 7% for 25 years creates roughly $27,000 in future wealth. You can have a wonderful wedding and build wealth simultaneously — but only if you proposal intentionally from the start.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Sources indicate that before finalizing your wedding budget, run the compound interest math on any amount you are considering spending. A $30,000 wedding invested at 7% for 30 years becomes roughly $228,000. A $15,000 wedding invested at 7% for 30 years becomes roughly $114,000. This is not an argument against celebrating — it is an argument for spending intentionally on what matters to you and cutting everything else. The couple who spends $15,000 on a joyful celebration and invests the other $15,000 gets both the wedding and a significant head start on financial independence.

No. Wedding debt is one of the worst forms of consumer debt because it funds a single day with no residual asset value. The average couple who finances their wedding on credit cards at 22% interest turns a $20,000 wedding into a $28,000 expense over 4 years of payments. Set a cash budget and stick to it.

Recent findings suggest that any contribution from parents is a gift, not an obligation. If parents offer to contribute, have an honest conversation about the total amount and whether it comes with expectations about the guest list or style. It has been revealed that set your budget privately as a couple before discussing with family. Present it as a decision, not a discussion.   • The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Recent findings suggest that today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to proposal for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

According to recent reports, but making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

It has been revealed that project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many upcoming science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Industry observers note that figure 1. Fresh public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

Recent findings suggest that when organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an key part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved crucial in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Industry observers note that making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an key first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

Sources indicate that the inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

In a recent development, participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Sources indicate that teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

Recent findings suggest that the CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or organization building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding upcoming expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

Sources indicate that while we are excited about these upcoming features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this revision. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

It has been revealed that this pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the upcoming multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New agentic AI solution leverages APIs to collect compliance evidence from systems and applies it to over 30 frameworks with no duplicate work.

According to recent reports, SEATTLE, November 18, 2026 — Strike Graph, the enterprise AI-native governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) management platform, today announced a latest integration solution that seamlessly connects to any software API to automatically collect compliance evidence from it. With Integration AI, organizations using the Strike Graph platform are no longer limited to a fixed integration catalog. They simply indicate the system they are using and Strike Graph builds a native integration that pulls compliance evidence from it automatically.

Once connected via an API, the Strike Graph platform employs an AI research agent to read the vendor’s public API documentation and draft a build specification. Concurrently, a second AI agent builds the complete integration across Strike Graph’s backend, user interface, and evidence pipeline. Integrations connect API-to-API, and customers never install agents or software inside their own infrastructure, which is critical for maintaining enterprise-grade security.

Related:It's a Bot World. We're Just Living in It.

“For compliance to be successful, access to evidence must be quick, easy, and continuous, but integration with existing tools often presents a challenge,” said Justin Beals, CEO and founder of Strike Graph. “Integration AI has empowered Strike Graph to overcome those roadblocks and accomplish all three of those requirements at once. If it has an API, Strike Graph can collect evidence from it. Furthermore, since Strike Graph’s evidence model is graph-based, evidence from a newly built integration automatically counts toward every framework a customer pursues, including SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, and CMMC, with no duplicate work.”.

In a recent development, as with all Strike Graph evidence collection integrations, Integration AI builds secure integrations that are restricted to read-only operations by default. Each one carries an endpoint allowlist that ratifies against the vendor’s real API documentation, which guarantees evidence collection can observe a customer’s systems but never change or impact them.

Strike Graph keeps strict separation where credentials are never touched by Integration AI.The build process works outside of the core governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) program itself, building the connection with no access to any customer secrets. Credentials and other sensitive data live in a securely managed secrets vault, and the build spec is scanned and automatically rejected if any credentials are detected in it.

Sources indicate that with Integration AI, vendor documentation is treated strictly as data and never as instructions, which blocks prompt-injection attempts hidden in third-party content. The AI build environment holds no publishing rights, and a separate locked-down step does the publishing.

Related:Satellites Have a Ground-Level Cybersecurity Problem.

Sources indicate that builds sit behind an approver allowlist and a kill switch, and humans are always in the loop to review the research initiative before build starts, after code has been written, and before anything is deployed to production. The AI can only propose changes, not ship them, and every integration requires a human engineering review.

Once built, Integration AI runs evidence scripts in self-contained isolated sandbox environments with no shared code paths, so a flaw in one integration can’t spread to another.

In a recent development, integration AI is available to Strike Graph customers today. For more information, visit www.strikegraph.com.

About Strike GraphStrike Graph is an AI-native GRC tech giant empowering organizations to eliminate redundant compliance work, accelerate audits, and achieve trust. Strike Graph's next-generation platform transforms GRC through its purpose-built graph-based architecture, patent-pending agentic evidence validation technology, Verify AI, intelligent recommendation engine, Security Assistant, and dynamic mapping across 30+ compliance frameworks. Built with privacy-first principles, Strike Graph hosts its own AI models rather than relying on third-party services, ensuring customer data remains secure and siloed. Founded in 2020 by technologist and serial entrepreneur Justin Beals and backed by top-tier investors, Strike Graph has helped hundreds of organizations reduce compliance timelines by more than 86%. Learn more at strikegraph.com.

#161112. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1299 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Transformers Model Integration Contracts

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1299 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, on July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5.
  • It has been revealed that when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them.
  • Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is major: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

It has been revealed that when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is major: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Industry observers note that our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

In a recent development, model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

In a recent development, transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:.

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

It has been revealed that for example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:.

In a recent development, it also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

In a recent development, A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

Industry observers note that we also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

According to recent reports, the Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:.

Industry observers note that it drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

Sources indicate that we used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

Sources indicate that with random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:.

Recent findings suggest that the Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:.

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Recent findings suggest that want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities.
  • In a recent development, our goal is to be exhaustive.
  • As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

In a recent development, our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

According to recent reports, results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:.

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:.

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:.

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:.

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.
