Where scientists draw the line on AI agents

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1667 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished.
  • These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science.
  • To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced. A researcher automating part of a lab protocol needs confidence that the system respects physical safety constraints, such as temperature limits or material toxicity, while a researcher working with human-participant data needs assurance that a system protects participants' privacy and limits who can access their information. Researchers also need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work.

These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings.

To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies.

Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used.

According to recent reports, one of our main findings concerns trust. Across the interviews, we identified five dimensions of scientific trust: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency. Together, they reflect concerns that go beyond whether an AI system produces a correct answer. Researchers also need to understand how an answer was reached, protect sensitive information, recognize bias, and determine who is charged with verifying and standing behind AI-assisted findings. These are matters of responsible conduct of research.

Another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized.

A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge.

In a recent development, for many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing new ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually.

But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs.

Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis.

But checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way.

Recent findings suggest that our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows.

Recent findings suggest that these examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks.

These evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like.

Verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process?

An early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?”.

According to recent reports, some participants were concerned that AI-assisted research could diminish learning, though the value of automation depends in part on the researcher and the task. An experienced scientist may reasonably delegate a familiar procedure to save time, while someone still learning that procedure may benefit from doing the work themselves.

Participants also drew different boundaries around activities involving intellectual contribution. One biologist refused to use AI to generate research ideas, considering that a responsibility to retain personally. Others were more open to AI-assisted ideation or writing. An anthropologist, for example, argued that some sections of scientific papers, particularly routine descriptions of methods and results, are formulaic enough to benefit from automation.

In a recent development, even researchers who tried AI for writing sometimes reconsidered. One political scientist described using Claude to help revise a manuscript, then deciding to rewrite the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear. “I don’t know what was AI and what was me,” the researcher said.

Sources indicate that context mattered, too. Having AI critique a manuscript before submission was viewed favorably by some participants, while using it to review another researcher's unpublished work raised concerns. The distinction involves more than technical capability; peer review carries responsibilities around confidentiality, attribution, and the fair evaluation of others' research.

Sources indicate that these disagreements suggest that responsible automation cannot be defined by a universal list of acceptable and unacceptable tasks. Scientific fields have different norms, and individual researchers may have different goals even when performing similar work.

The same tension applies to safeguards built into AI systems. One political scientist described how content restrictions that prevent AI tools from discussing certain topics could interfere with legitimate research on political violence or human rights violations. Meanwhile, participants working with sensitive human-subject data wanted stronger guarantees about privacy, access, and how information would be used.

Sources indicate that both are valid concerns. An agent that acts without sufficient safeguards could expose confidential data or produce harmful results, while one that’s constrained too broadly could prevent scientists from pursuing legitimate lines of inquiry.

This is why scientific communities need a meaningful role in shaping the boundaries of AI assistance. Developers need to understand not only which activities an agent can perform, but which decisions researchers want to retain and where safeguards are necessary—as well as where those safeguards might obstruct valuable work.

Our findings point toward an approach to scientific AI development that starts with the people who will use the technology.

Recent findings suggest that researchers should be able to examine an agent's contributions, determine which work to assign, and preserve opportunities to develop their own expertise. Achieving that will require technical features such as transparent records of agent actions and granular data controls, alongside evaluations informed by the standards and practices of different scientific communities.

It will also require continued collaboration. Our study is exploratory; the findings come from interviews with 17 US-based scientists, not a representative survey of scientific opinion or an empirical evaluation of specific AI agents. Participants discussed both the generative AI tools they use today and what they anticipate from more autonomous systems. Their perspectives identify crucial concerns and design priorities, rather than establishing a consensus about how AI should be used in science.

Still, they offer a path forward. At Ai2, we believe AI can accelerate scientific discovery while preserving the openness, reproducibility, and independent scrutiny that make research trustworthy. Through our broader efforts to develop and evaluate scientific agents, we aim to put those principles into practice. That means working with scientists to identify worthwhile uses for agents and translating their concerns into concrete evaluations, in addition to making it easier to understand both what these systems accomplish and how they accomplish it.

In a recent development, the promise of scientific AI isn't simply that researchers can pass off more work. It's that they can pursue questions that might otherwise be out of reach while retaining the knowledge, judgment, and agency needed to make discoveries that are their own.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

Industry observers note that A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:.

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Recent findings suggest that blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

It has been revealed that and that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

In a recent development, blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Industry observers note that although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Recent findings suggest that tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

In a recent development, blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

It has been revealed that blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

In a recent development, have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

In a recent development, instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

According to recent reports, blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a organization's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Industry observers note that yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of customers constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Sources indicate that coinbase Global is presently the biggest blockchain tech giant in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

In a recent development, blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency.

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

In a recent development, blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. Tech Report: Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2346 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Part 1: Understanding swarms and training to communicate.
  • This is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers.
  • That's what we'll do in this series!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Part 1: Understanding swarms and training to communicate.

This is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers. We (us, the community, you) want to build our own agent swarms because they're exciting, challenging, and increasingly capable. Furthermore, it would be extremely cool if we could train our own agents to work in a swarm. And exponentially cool if those swarms used small and affordable models.

That's what we'll do in this series! Each blog post will include some context on building swarms, alongside reproducible examples that you can run on Hugging Face Jobs. This post's example takes about five hours on two H200s, which costs roughly $50.

Multi-Agent Systems are hard to get working. Adding agents changes the agent's context, the budget, and in turn the complexity of the whole system. Mixing agents' context together through communication is not an inherent performance boost compared to a single agent. The model needs to learn to communicate through training. How do we define what models should learn? And which model weights do we update when we're dealing with many agents?

It has been revealed that in this series, we'll work through those problems with an educational overview and practical examples. Each post will introduce a question, build a small system, and examine what happens and how you can reproduce it. This first example starts with four agents, a shared language model, and a simple verifiable task. It's ideal to implement yourself, to tinker with, and to learn from.

First, we'll start off with some context on swarms.

In a recent development, we've heard a lot about swarms over the past few months, both good and bad. In September this year, OpenAI announced that a swarm of roughly 10,000 agents had found a singularity in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, one of the Millennium Prize problems. A smaller group of nearly 100 agents had already disproved regularity for the unforced 3D Euler equations, a closely related open problem.

In a recent development, but swarms don't always work on the problems we want them to. METR's investigation of the Hugging Face incident found that around 1,200 OpenAI agents, which were supposed to be isolated, had found a way to exchange over 70,000 messages and files. Around 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face while looking for ways to fool their benchmark's scorer, without instruction to do so.

A major swarm isn't, by itself, evidence that cooperation helped. Noam Brown estimates that less than 10% of the Navier-Stokes result came from multi-agent cooperation. In Anthropic's vulnerability-finding experiment, coordinated agents found more bugs than independent agents, but also searched more code and used more tokens. When the comparison was restricted to the same directories, the results per million tokens were about the same.

According to recent reports, start with the simplest case. If four agents each try a task independently, the chance that at least one gets it right is higher than with a single attempt, as long as we can tell which answer is correct. That makes a useful baseline for a multi-agent system, but it doesn't show that the agents helped each other. They may simply have had more tries.

Four attempts also cost four times as much. So the fairer comparison is at an equal budget: if each of four agents gets a quarter of the total tokens, can they still beat one agent that spends all of them? We can only find out by testing, because the answer depends on the task, the model and how the work is divided.

This series keeps asking one question: when agents communicate, does it actually help, or are we just spending more compute?

We understand that question through this simple expectation.

We'll treat agent count as a scaling dimension, alongside tokens and model size. Sometimes adding agents will help. Sometimes coordination will consume the budget we hoped to save. The point is to measure both. We won't start with 10,000 agents. We'll start with a small team on a task that we can check easily.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning has studied cooperation and competition long before language models were called swarms.

A single agent's task is a Markov decision process: observe, act, get a reward. In a team, everyone shares the reward, but each agent sees only part of the world. This is a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process: teammates, but no one sees the whole picture.

Sources indicate that this creates three practical problems. First, teammates keep changing while each agent learns. Second, credit assignment: when the team succeeds, which actions deserve the credit? A winning team can include weak actions, and we may end up rewarding them. Third, a message changes what other agents observe, so communication is part of the policy we're training.

According to recent reports, A common solution is centralized training with decentralized execution: training uses information from the whole team, but each agent acts only on its own observations. Our first example follows this pattern with a shared team reward.

It has been revealed that agents can also be organized in different ways. Two useful starting points are:.

It has been revealed that A hierarchy. A lead agent assigns work to workers and collects their results. Anthropic's Research system works this way, with a separate context for each worker. Kimi K2.5's PARL trains only the orchestrator and keeps the subagents frozen, so training a multi-agent system doesn't mean updating every component. See Anthropic's system description and Kimi's technical blog.

A distributed team. Peers send each other messages and decide when to read their inboxes. No lead agent assigns the actions. This is the setup we'll use here, following the information-aggregation task in s³: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL.

It has been revealed that we'll reproduce the information-sharing task from Simple Scaling of Swarms because it's interpretable and straightforward to implement. Four agents share a small language model and learn to pool what each of them knows.

Each agent receives one integer from 1 to 99. It knows its own assignment and its teammates' names. It does not initially know the other agents' numbers. For example, four private assignments might be "five", "twenty-six", "five" and "seventy-eight". Duplicates stay in the list, so a correct final answer is:.

According to recent reports, the team succeeds when at least one agent submits the complete, correctly sorted list. One correct answer is enough; success does not require all four agents to answer correctly. An agent cannot reliably infer the other private assignments without information from its teammates.

Sources indicate that this means the task does not yet test Figure 1 directly. Each agent holds information the others need, so a single agent, or a team without messaging, cannot succeed however many retries it gets. Instead, the task tests the precondition behind Figure 1: can a small shared policy learn to communicate at all, and how many tokens does that cost? A later post moves to a task that a single agent can solve alone, where the matched-budget comparison is meaningful.

The main communication tools are message(to, text), read_messages(), and check_notifications(). A notification tells an agent that unread messages exist; reading its inbox makes their contents available. Agents can send direct messages or broadcast to everyone.

We defined a four-agent system using one shared Qwen3-0.6B policy, with separate contexts and private inputs. We are not training four different models. The prompt explains the task and the tools, including the need to share assignments.

Industry observers note that in this post, a team means one episode: four agents attempting one problem once. A successful team receives a reward reduced by the tokens it uses. A failed team receives zero:.

For illustration, a correct team using half its allowance receives 0.875. There is no separate reward for sending messages. The incentive is to solve the task while using fewer generated tokens.

In a recent development, for every training problem, we collect eight independent team attempts. Their rewards are normalized within that group. An attempt that does better than its group average gets a positive advantage; one that does worse gets a negative advantage. Every agent in the same team receives that team's advantage, including an agent whose own final answer was wrong.

Industry observers note that in TRL, each agent's sampled tokens form a training row. Its incoming messages and tool results provide context. The loss is averaged within each team and then across teams, so longer conversations do not give a team more weight.

Our results come from the original experiment, which used 256 team attempts per upgrade (32 problems with eight attempts each). The walkthrough uses TRL's default of --teams-per-update 128, which works out to about 150 team attempts per update.

Over 75 steps, training success rose from 6.6% to 82.3%, comparing the first and last five updates. At checkpoint 75, the four-agent team solved 26 of 32 held-out problems (81.25%). The paper reports 93.2% four-agent success after 200 updates.

Industry observers note that the team also used 37.4% fewer tokens per attempt, falling from about 13k to 8k. This improvement accompanied more active information sharing: broadcasts increased from 2.38 to 5.73 per team, even as total token use fell.

In a recent development, the team also used fewer tokens later in training. Comparing the first five updates with updates 71–75:.

That is a 37.4% reduction in generated tokens per training team between those windows. At batch 75 itself, the mean was 7,624 tokens per team. These are training measurements; we did not retain held-out token-efficiency measurements for the trained checkpoint.

It has been revealed that notice that fewer tokens did not mean fewer messages. More agents began participating but broadcasting became more common, rather than direct messaging. Generated tokens include reasoning and tool calls as well as message bodies, so message count alone does not tell us how much text the team produced.

Sources indicate that no agent can solve the problem alone, so the closest equivalent of "a single agent with more retries" is the untrained team with more retries. The training data already contains this comparison. Each update collects eight attempts per problem, and the task's answers are easy to check, so we can count a problem as solved when any of its eight attempts succeeded. Early in training, that count gives the untrained team's best-of-8 success rate:.

With eight retries, the untrained team solves fewer than half the problems and spends about 13 times as many tokens as one attempt from the trained team. Read this as an estimate. Both rows use training problems rather than held-out ones, and updates 2–5 already sample from a slightly trained policy.

The model is small, but the rollouts are not. Each update generates millions of tokens of agent conversation at contexts of up to 40k tokens. We used one H200 for the trainer and seven H200s running vLLM rollout engines to get through those rollouts promptly, and kept each worker's eight attempts together. The walkthrough below runs the same task on two GPUs. Here are the infra details:.

Sources indicate that the figures above describe our original 75-revision experiment. In this walkthrough we'll run TRL's swarm example on Hugging Face Jobs. One H200 serves the shared Qwen3-0.6B policy with vLLM and a second H200 trains it.

Industry observers note that sign in with a Hugging Face account that can run Jobs and create buckets. Replace YOUR_USERNAME with your Hub username.

Use a fresh bucket for each run so earlier measurements stay available.

Save the script below as train-swarm.sh in your current directory.

The command below sends its contents to the job. Inside the job, vLLM serves the shared policy on GPU 0. GPU 1 runs TRL's async_grpo_s3_aggregation.py for 50 updates with Trackio. TRL's evaluate.py scores the base model and checkpoint 50 on the same 192 held-out problems. That is a larger set than the 32-problem checks in our results, which gives tighter error bars. The job saves both scores, the checkpoint, Trackio data and the exact Git commit to your bucket.

One TRL rollout contains a whole team conversation. The trainer compares eight attempts at the same problem and gives all four agents in an attempt the same advantage. Each update uses about 150 team attempts. TRL packs micro-batches by token count rather than by team, so the --teams-per-update 128 setting is approximate. The --report-to trackio flag records training metrics at every update.

Sources indicate that this shorter run is cheaper than our original experiment, and it stops earlier on the learning curve. TRL's run of this example took about 4.8 hours on two H100s and reached 60.9% held-out success at checkpoint 50.

Sources indicate that to run closer to our original experiment, change the training flags to --updates 75 --teams-per-update 256 --concurrent-teams 256, replace checkpoint-50 with checkpoint-75 in the script, and raise the job's --timeout to 24h. That is three times as many rollouts. The two codebases still differ in details such as the system prompt, so expect similar results rather than an exact replication.

Industry observers note that once the job completes, sync the bucket to a local folder. It holds the two evaluation files, the Trackio data, the TRL revision and the checkpoint-50 weights, which are the largest download. In the dashboard, compare team/success, team/messages and team/tokens over training. The job logs also give the held-out success rate for the base model and checkpoint 50. Each line of base.jsonl or trained.jsonl records one of those evaluation attempts.

This first example gives us a small environment, a shared reward and a policy that improves at pooling private information. It also shows why success, token use and communication structure need to be read together. At 75 updates, the team is solving most checked problems, but it has not converged to the cleanest communication pattern.

In the coming examples, we'll take a step back from training and look at how we evaluate and analyze swarms.

For now, we have something concrete to build on: four small agents, one trainable policy, a checkable task, and a reproducible way to examine what the team learned.

#160995. I built an open source permissions layer for AI agents. Here is what it does and what it can't do.

I built an open source permissions layer for AI agents. Here is what it does and what it can't do.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (571 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI agents call tools: they read files, send email, hit internal APIs, run code.
  • In a recent development, security teams are starting to ask the obvious questions.
  • I built Agent Tessera to answer them without tying you to one LLM provider or agent framework.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI agents call tools: they read files, send email, hit internal APIs, run code. In most codebases, what an agent is allowed to do is whatever its API keys allow, and the record of what it did is scattered application logs.

In a recent development, security teams are starting to ask the obvious questions. Which agents exist? What can each one call? Who approved the risky action? Can you prove what happened? Right now most teams can't answer.

I built Agent Tessera to answer them without tying you to one LLM provider or agent framework. It is open source (Apache 2.0).

You write what an agent may do in a short YAML file:.

You mark your tools, or wrap your LLM client:.

Industry observers note that anything the policy doesn't allow is denied before the function runs, and the decision lands in an audit log. Each event includes the hash of the previous one, so editing the log afterwards is detectable:.

Enforce locally, govern centrally. The SDK evaluates the policy inside your process. There's no network call per decision, so it is fast and keeps working if the control plane is down. The optional server registers agents, challenges short-lived credentials, signs policy bundles (the SDK rejects bundles with a bad signature), collects audit events, and has a kill switch and a web console.

Default deny, one decision order. Suspension and kill switches come first, then explicit denies, delegation limits, the allow-rule check (no matching rule means deny), rate limits and quotas, and approvals last. There's one order, documented, and table-tested.

It has been revealed that plain YAML policies. I deliberately did not adopt a general policy language. The people who review agent permissions are often not the people who write the agent, and a short YAML file is something they can actually read.

Industry observers note that provider neutral. Adapters for OpenAI (and Azure), Anthropic, Bedrock, Gemini, and LiteLLM; integrations for LangChain/LangGraph, MCP, the OpenAI Agents SDK, and CrewAI. A registry lets you add your own client.

Minimal dependencies. The core needs httpx, pydantic, pyjwt, and pyyaml. Provider SDKs are optional extras.

This matters more than the feature list.

It enforces policy inside the agent's process, on the calls you route through it. If code calls a provider's HTTP API directly, nothing checks that call. There is an opt-in detect_bypass mode that records such calls for the main providers, but it only detects them. And a hostile process can disable the SDK outright. It's a guardrail for agents you trust to be mostly well-behaved, not a sandbox. For untrusted code, pair it with container isolation and egress rules.

It also doesn't track data between agents (agent A can pass B something B couldn't read), and it doesn't detect prompt injection; it limits what an injected agent can do through governed calls.

The full list is on the threat model page.

Recent findings suggest that A stable 1.0 API, agent-to-agent identity with A2A Agent Cards, and sub-agent spawning with permission attenuation. Later: a gateway mode for agents you can't modify, and a TypeScript SDK. SAML, SCIM, Slack/Teams approvals, and SIEM connectors aren't built; contributions are welcome.

Sources indicate that the README quickstart takes about two minutes and needs no API key. I'd like to hear what is missing, especially from people who have to answer "what can this agent do?" for a security review.

Repo: https://github.com/agent-tessera/agent-tessera Docs: https://agent-tessera.dev/.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face. It lets you track prompt processing and text generation performance across llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations, so you can explore how local inference performs on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware.

Local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve. We want those changes to be easy to inspect for any AMD developer: pick a hardware, a model and a build, compare quantizations, and follow performance over time. The benchmark workflow and underlying results are public, so you can also inspect how we benchmark inference performance.

Sources indicate that you can choose Hardware, Model, and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar. The current hardware choices are Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201).

The dashboard shows two separate tests, both measured in tokens per second:.

Recent findings suggest that both tests start at context depth zero (n_depth=0). PP512 measures processing 512 input tokens without generation; TG128 measures generating 128 tokens without a pre-existing context. The plotted value is the mean throughput (avg_ts). These are useful reference workloads, while the Context scaling tab lets you explore token generation throughput as the context grows.

We benchmark the prebuilt binaries distributed through llama-install.sh, the build and installation project behind llama.app. The public gfx1151 and gfx1201 workflows are scheduled weekly and run the standard benchmarks using the llama-bench tool with Flash Attention on and off, with 10 repetitions per configuration.

It has been revealed that the model set evolves and right now includes Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. Available GGUF formats include Q4_K_M, Q8_0, other quantizations, and higher-precision formats such as BF16 and F16.

Recent findings suggest that the explorer reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket on Hugging Face. The data source link beside the chart title opens the folder for the selected build, hardware, and model.

Standard results use ///.jsonl. Workload sweeps use the same folder -tg.jsonl filename.

Use them to investigate a result, make your own charts, or compare with a local run.

Sources indicate that thanks to the AMD team for providing test infrastructure and helping validate the setup! Try the dashboard, inspect the data, and let us know which models and workloads you would like to see next.

Tech Report: Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

📅 01 Jun 2022 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2269 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Blogspot

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that there are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business.
  • Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies.
  • Industry observers note that an affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing1. What is affiliate marketing? Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!2. What is an affiliate program? An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers. Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping? Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands. 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing? Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action. 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices? Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a significant opportunity.7. Where do I find qualified publishers? The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement? An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases. 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing? Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.10. What is a super affiliate? A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program. Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.11. How do we track publisher sales activity? Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard. 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries? Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.13. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Spinning up a Single-Node OpenShift (SNO) cluster on AWS for training or lab environments doesn't always require heavy Terraform or CloudFormation scaffolding.
  • Because AWS AMIs do not support "Bootstrap-in-Place" installations, you briefly start with a temporary bootstrap instance before the master node takes over.
  • Always run the installer in a clean, empty directory—leftover hidden state files from earlier attempts can cause certificate or SNI mismatches.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spinning up a Single-Node OpenShift (SNO) cluster on AWS for training or lab environments doesn't always require heavy Terraform or CloudFormation scaffolding. With User-Provisioned Infrastructure (UPI), you stay close to the actual mechanics and see every stage of the cluster coming up.

Because AWS AMIs do not support "Bootstrap-in-Place" installations, you briefly start with a temporary bootstrap instance before the master node takes over.

Always run the installer in a clean, empty directory—leftover hidden state files from earlier attempts can cause certificate or SNI mismatches. Also back up your install-config.yaml, as the installer removes it during setup:.

(Add your Red Hat pull secret and SSH public key in the final two lines.).

To allow the ingress router and image registry to run on the single node, set mastersSchedulable to true before generating the Ignition files:.

Because AWS EC2 User-Data is limited to 16 KB and the generated .ign files are larger, host bootstrap.ign and master.ign on your Nginx web server and pass small JSON pointer configs into EC2 User-Data:.

Once the cluster is up, tighten your security group rules, remove the Ignition files from the web server (as they contain sensitive data), and raise the DNS TTL back up. For dynamic PVC provisioning, install Red Hat LVM Storage (LVMS) via a Subscription in the openshift-storage namespace.

For workshops and lab environments, the UPI route on AWS is great when you want visibility into bootstrap, cutover, and storage without hiding behind black-box automation.

For the full step-by-step walkthrough, check out the detailed guide in the repository: openshift_single_node_aws_upi_installation_guide.md.

#160990. Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1572 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1572 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanks to our partnership with AWS, we were lucky enough to get access to a Trainium3 machine (trn3.48xlarge, 64 NeuronCores) for a month.
  • With five days left, I allowed myself a little fun.
  • I picked LTX-2.5 from Lightricks, which generates video and sound together.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanks to our partnership with AWS, we were lucky enough to get access to a Trainium3 machine (trn3.48xlarge, 64 NeuronCores) for a month. We spent most of the month testing Hugging Face models on it, and getting more of them to work.

With five days left, I allowed myself a little fun. When you have a Ferrari, every now and then you want to take it out on the track. So I asked myself: what if I tried to generate videos?

I picked LTX-2.5 from Lightricks, which generates video and sound together. By the end, once the models were loaded, a 10-second clip with sound took 22 to 23 s to generate, on half of the machine. Here is the result.

It has been revealed that I had two goals. The first was to see how easy it is to generate videos with diffusers on Trainium3. Not the simple clips from the examples: I wanted to make short films from a script, closer to a real use case, like drafting a movie. The second was performance. I wanted to get close to what you get with CUDA, or with LTX's own API.

For CUDA, I found no real figure to compare against. The only one is LTX's claim of 6.8 s for a 10-second 720p clip on four B200 GPUs, with no detail on how it was measured. So I set CUDA aside and compared with LTX's online API instead, which LTX states makes a 10-second 1080p clip in 23.7 s. In the end, the setup matches it, and even beats it by about a second: 22 to 23 s for a 10-second clip at 2048×1024, once the models are loaded, on half of the machine. Not bad, considering how little time I had to optimize the pipelines.

The input is a film: a JSON list of shots, each with a name and a prompt, much like a storyboard. LTX-2.5 does better with long prompts, so each prompt is a paragraph on the style, the subject, the motion, the camera, the light and the sound. Here is the seal film's file, with the prompts shortened:.

In a recent development, each shot has a name and a prompt, and can have a seed, to keep the take I picked among several. Shots are chained with two keys. This chaining is the point, since prompts alone do not keep a subject from one shot to the next:.

A shot can also be trimmed, or have a caption drawn over it.

Making a film from shots works like animation, which has two ways to go. Straight ahead, each shot continues the one before. Pose to pose, you make the key shot first, until you get one you like; then the shots before it end on its first frames (to), and the shots after it start from its last frames (from). When a film builds up to a payoff (the moment everything was leading to), the payoff is the key shot. I found this order by trial and error, and made the seal film pose to pose, starting from iceberg.

According to recent reports, the payoff is iceberg: the iceberg rolls over, and its wave drenches the seal. nap, the sleeping seal, ends on the first 9 frames of iceberg (to), so that the seal, the floe and the iceberg stay the same into the payoff. shake starts from the last 25 frames of iceberg (from): the dripping seal shakes off the water and flops down on the floe. The dream is made on its own, and a cut joins it to the rest.

Industry observers note that on the diffusers side, three pipelines share the models of LTX-2.5. LTX2Pipeline makes the shots from their prompt alone, and LTX2ConditionPipeline makes the shots that start or end on frames of another shot. These two follow the two-stage distilled recipe of the model card: 8 steps, then the third pipeline, LTX2LatentUpsamplePipeline, upscales the latents ×2 before 3 final steps.

The diffusers pipelines do all of the generation. The film part is about 160 lines of Python on top: read the film file, order the shots so each keyframe exists before the shot that needs it, and cut the frames to hand over; then trim, caption, even out the sound and assemble the film. The code is in dacorvo/video-generation. The films I kept are in the dacorvo/video-generation bucket, with their JSON files: the seal, the fox, and the goat, which trims two of its shots and draws a caption over its payoff.

Out of the box, the model does not run on the NeuronCores: the transformer does not fit on one, and diffusers has no plan to split it. The first attempt that ran (the model card's pipeline, with the transformer split over 4 cores and a few patches) took about 5 min 20 s for a 10-second clip, and the NeuronCores were actually computing for only about 45 s of it. What's more, the target resolution was out of reach.

Getting there took three kinds of work: making the model run on the NeuronCores (requires tensor parallelism), splitting it over more of them (sequence parallelism), and making the host keep up with them.

In a recent development, most of the fixes below are on the device, and that is where most of the effort went. The biggest end-to-end savings came from the host: the low-hanging fruit, since that is obviously where the waste was.

Three problems were never explained: the transformer compiled as one graph returned NaN at one size, the first shot that ends on keyframes was slow in each newly introduced process (even with every graph in the cache), and the latent upsampler fails to load next to the transformer, so it stays on the CPU.

Industry observers note that some of this is being fixed upstream. diffusers#15420 (open) fixes the LTX-2 pipelines, which would make the second workaround above unnecessary. diffusers#14725 (still open) brings tensor and context parallelism into one ParallelConfig, and a _tp_plan for LTX-2.5 is planned.

According to recent reports, on the performance side, once the models are loaded, a 10-second 2048×1024 clip with sound takes 22 to 23 s. That rivals LTX's paid API, on half of the instance. A service would keep its processes up, as they take about 3 minutes to load the models, and 80 s for their first clip.

Sources indicate that on the feature side, diffusers has what it takes to draft a movie. The shots come from prompts, and keep their subject from one shot to the next by starting or ending on frames of other shots. Takes differ by their seed, and the film file keeps the one I picked. Re-run with the same code and film file, and you get the same film back, byte for byte. A shot can also start from an image, such as a storyboard frame or a character sheet, which the condition pipeline takes the same way as frames (I did not try it in a film).

According to recent reports, LTX calls LTX-2.5 a world model, with robotics as an emerging use. Robots, cars and drones learn from videos of what their cameras see, and a world model can make more of them, including events too rare or too risky to film. So I also tried it on real footage, with the same code: a shot can start from the first second of a real camera clip and invent what happens next. One frame was not enough, as the model cannot tell from it how fast things move.

Here is the head camera of a Fourier GR1-T2 humanoid robot (a clip from NVIDIA's GR1-100), looking down at a table. In the real 6-second clip, the robot's left hand picks an orange from a plate and drops it in a tray. The model only sees the first second of that clip (the hands raised, before anything moves) and invents the rest. What really happened, next to its invention:.

Same scene, same pick: the model invents the grab on its own, and keeps the table, the hands and the fruit consistent with the real footage. More interesting are the events that did not happen. From the same second, with only the prompt changed, a person leans over and grabs the orange too, and the human hand and the robot hand carry it to the tray together. Five takes, with the real footage first:.

The person's gestures and timing differ in each take, and the robot's arm adapts to them. That is the appeal for training: not one continuation of a clip, but a distribution of them, each reproducible from its film file and seed.

The robotics folder of the bucket has the five takes with their JSON files, and a second example from the front camera of a car in a snowstorm (Boreas), where the alternate event is slush thrown on the lens by a passing truck. Asked to make the car accelerate instead, the model kept its speed: the prompt does not override what the first second of footage already implies.

Sources indicate that these videos follow prompts, not the robot's or car's commands: a training setup would need generation conditioned on those actions. For that, a team fine-tunes the pre-trained checkpoint of LTX-2.5 on the frames and actions of its own robots.

The Ferrari made it around the track, on half of its cylinders.

  • If you've ever wanted to run a production-grade retrieval-augmented chatbot on your own infrastructure-on a laptop, a homelab server, or a single VPS-this is the stack I'd recommend in 2025: LangChain for orchestration, ChromaDB for vector storage, and Ollama for the LLM runtime.
  • Let me walk you through building one end-to-end, including the parts most tutorials skip: chunking strategy, retrieval tuning, conversation memory, caching, monitoring, and Docker deployment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I built my first RAG system two years ago. It cost me $400 in OpenAI API calls before I realized the team was querying the same 50 documents repeatedly. We were paying per token for retrieval over a static knowledge base. That's when it clicked-most RAG use cases don't need a frontier model in the cloud. They need a decent local model, a vector store that doesn't require a PhD to operate, and a framework that gets out of your way.

If you've ever wanted to run a production-grade retrieval-augmented chatbot on your own infrastructure-on a laptop, a homelab server, or a single VPS-this is the stack I'd recommend in 2025: LangChain for orchestration, ChromaDB for vector storage, and Ollama for the LLM runtime. No API keys. No per-token billing. No data leaving your network.

Let me walk you through building one end-to-end, including the parts most tutorials skip: chunking strategy, retrieval tuning, conversation memory, caching, monitoring, and Docker deployment.

For the LLM, I'll use Llama 3.1 8B through this guide. It's a solid default-small enough to run on a laptop, capable enough for most RAG tasks. If you have more RAM, swap in qwen2.5:14b or mistral-nemo and the code stays the same.

Here's the request flow for our chatbot:.

The pipeline is straightforward:.

The ingestion pipeline (run separately) looks like:.

Sources indicate that keep chroma_db/ on a persistent volume in production. Lose that directory and you'll re-embed your entire corpus, which for large datasets means hours of compute and a window where the chatbot returns zero results.

Install Ollama from ollama.com or via the install script:.

Recent findings suggest that I prefer nomic-embed-text over OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small for local setups. It's a 137M parameter model, runs in milliseconds on CPU, and produces embeddings competitive with proprietary options on standard benchmarks. If you need multilingual support, swap in bge-m3.

It has been revealed that embedding the same chunk twice is wasted compute. LangChain supports caching out of the box:.

Industry observers note that this is also useful during development. When you're iterating on prompts or chunking strategies, caching the LLM calls saves you from regenerating answers for unchanged contexts-which on a local 8B model still takes 5-10 seconds per query and adds up fast when you're running evals.

In a recent development, I've used all three in production. LangChain wins on developer ergonomics and the size of the integration ecosystem. LlamaIndex has better ingestion pipelines for complex document types and a more opinionated (in a good way) approach to retrieval. Haystack is overkill unless you're building a search product at scale.

A breakdown for a typical small-team deployment (5-20 owners, ~10K documents):.

Industry observers note that total: roughly $50/month plus your time. Compare this to per-seat pricing on hosted RAG services, which typically run $20-50/user/month. For a 10-person team, you're looking at $200-500/month vs $50/month. The break-even point is usually around 3-5 consumers.

According to recent reports, the hidden cost is the ops burden. You're now responsible for uptime, updates, and incident response. If your team doesn't have bandwidth for that, the hosted option is worth the premium.

In a recent development, local RAG has crossed the threshold from "interesting experiment" to "production-ready default" in the last year. The combination of LangChain's orchestration, ChromaDB's simplicity, and Ollama's model runtime gives you a stack that's private, predictable in cost, and fast enough for real users.

Industry observers note that the hard part isn't the setup. It's the iteration-tuning chunk size, picking the right embedding model, deciding between semantic and hybrid search, and building the observability to know when things break. Start with the defaults in this article, ship it to your team, and refine based on actual usage. The first version will be 70% as good as it could be. That's enough to be useful, and the feedback loop will tell you what to fix next.

#160987. What breaks when your app scales to zero, and how to catch it

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1176 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

What breaks when your app scales to zero, and how to catch it

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1176 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Originally published on gregale.dev.
  • In a recent development, when an app scales to zero, whatever it kept only on its own machine is lost, such as files written to local disk or /tmp and sessions held in memory, and timers or background loops meant to run between requests stop.
  • By default the snapshot is taken from the deployment, right after the app becomes ready, not from the instance that parked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Originally published on gregale.dev. I build Gregale, so read this as a vendor's page. Competitor details come from each vendor's own docs, linked in the post. This post was written with AI assistance.

In a recent development, when an app scales to zero, whatever it kept only on its own machine is lost, such as files written to local disk or /tmp and sessions held in memory, and timers or background loops meant to run between requests stop. Anything in a database, in object storage or in the platform's crons and queues keeps working, because it lives outside the instance. On Gregale, every wake starts from the same snapshot and parking discards the instance's local state, so Gregale looks for the usual mistakes: it refuses stateful base images and VOLUME directives when it accepts a deploy, and records an audit row the first time an app writes to a database-shaped directory such as /data or /var/lib/postgresql. These stateless contract checks are generally available on every blueprint.

By default the snapshot is taken from the deployment, right after the app becomes ready, not from the instance that parked. So every wake starts from the same state, whatever the last instance did, and two instances restored at once start from the same memory. Two settings change what is in that memory; see What goes into the snapshot.

Only the first and last rows are things Gregale checks for you. The others are design choices; the table is the list to review before you deploy.

According to recent reports, at deploy. Gregale rejects a stateful base image when it accepts the deployment, with stateless_only_violation and HTTP 422: postgres:16, mysql:8, redis:7, mongo:7, mariadb, cockroach, cassandra, clickhouse and the rest. A source tarball with a VOLUME directive, or with top-level data/ or db/ directories, is rejected for the same reason.

It has been revealed that at runtime. Gregale watches the state-shaped directories in every instance: data/ and db/ under the app's working directory, plus /data, /db and /var/lib/postgresql, /var/lib/mysql, /var/lib/redis and the data directories of other databases. The first write to each file there records one stateless.advisory audit row. The check is advisory: the app keeps running, and the row is your signal that the data will not survive the next park.

It has been revealed that the first command lists recent rows; the second streams them live while you exercise the app. Each file is reported once per instance, and an instance reports at most 256 files.

Priming. Just before the snapshot is taken, Gregale sends up to 20 GET requests to the app's health check path, or to / when it declares none, so the snapshot holds a runtime that has already loaded and connected. Those requests run your code. If that path writes data, sends mail or calls a paid API, it does so up to 20 times per deploy. Declare a harmless warm-up path instead:.

Warm snapshots. Pro and Scale apps can opt in to a second snapshot, taken when an instance parks after it has served a few requests. It is reused by every later wake and every instance until the next deploy, and it carries whatever those first requests left in memory: sessions, caches, rate-limit counters, per-user data and files under /tmp. An app that keeps per-user state in memory must not use it. Apps created before 2026-11-10 on Pro or Scale were opted in by default; turn it off with:.

A connection opened at startup is captured in the snapshot, so a restored instance must reopen it. Declare an after_restore hook in gregale.yaml:.

After a restore, and after it has repaired the guest's clock and entropy, Gregale sends one POST to that path on the app's loopback listener. A 2xx answer lets the instance serve; a timeout or any other status discards it and Gregale cold-boots a fresh one instead. The timeout is 500 ms by default and at most 2 seconds. Check for a loopback peer and the X-Faas-After-Restore: 1 header in the handler: Gregale strips inbound x-faas-* headers at its public proxy, so a public caller cannot fake that marker. To close the connection before the snapshot is taken instead, add a before_checkpoint hook the same way. Redeploy after changing either: existing snapshots keep the configuration of the deployment that made them.

A Node or Python function declares the same thing as hooks in its handler file: init, beforeSnapshot and afterRestore (before_snapshot and after_restore in Python).

The writable layer on each instance is real disk, bounded by your plan's ephemeral disk ceiling, and writes to it are rate limited per plan:.

It has been revealed that each applies after a one-time burst of 256 MiB and 20,000 operations. Use the disk for work that ends with the request, such as unpacking an archive or rendering a file before you upload it.

Recent findings suggest that none of them keeps local files once the instance, execution environment or dyno is gone, and neither does Gregale. What Gregale adds is catching the mistake: at deploy for the clear cases, and with an audit row the first time a running app writes where it looks like it expects data to last.

Sources, checked 2026-11-27: Cloud Run container runtime contract, Lambda ephemeral storage, Heroku dynos.

According to recent reports, stateless contract checks are generally available on every proposal, Free included, and paused seconds are not billed on any plan. See Gregale pricing, Storage and How scaling to zero works.

What is lost when an app scales to zero?

Anything kept only on the instance: files written to local disk or /tmp, sessions and caches held in memory, and timers meant to run between requests. Data in a database, object storage or the platform’s crons and queues is kept.

How does Gregale warn me that my app writes data it will lose?

It rejects stateful base images such as postgres:16 and VOLUME directives at deploy with stateless_only_violation, and records a stateless.advisory audit row the first time an app writes to a database-shaped directory such as /data or /var/lib/postgresql.

How do I reconnect to my database after a snapshot restore?

Declare an after_restore hook in gregale.yaml. Gregale sends one POST to that path on the app’s loopback listener after repairing the clock and entropy; a 2xx answer lets the instance serve, anything else falls back to a cold boot.

Can a snapshot carry one user’s data into other instances?

In a recent development, only if you opt in to warm snapshots on Pro or Scale, or your app was created there before 2026-11-10. A warm snapshot is taken after an instance has served a few requests and keeps what they left in memory, so apps with per-user state in memory should turn it off with --no-warm-snapshot.

Recent findings suggest that not while it is paused. About a second after the last request, with nothing in flight, Gregale pauses the VM in memory, and paused seconds are not billed. An app that keeps itself busy with timers keeps running and is billed while it works.

Three Editors, One Photo: What Nano Banana, Seedream 4.0, and Qwen-Image-Edit Actually Do Differently
